stories.Headline: OpenTelemetry essential for AI observability interoperability
stories.Summary:
OpenTelemetry, the open standard for collecting telemetry data, is being presented as essential to AI observability interoperability, a theme covered by TechGig on October 27, 2026, and by The New Stack on October 26, 2026. The articles describe how engineering teams can standardise the data their AI systems produce so that it can be compared across different models, frameworks and providers. The coverage frames this as a way to deliver useful AI outcomes reliably and at lower cost. The reporting does not describe a single incident or a single event; it is an analysis of where AI monitoring is heading.

Standardised telemetry matters because AI applications involve many moving parts, including model providers, orchestration frameworks and evaluation services, and these change often. The TechGig piece says that shared conventions reduce the need for separate data models and integration work, and that they make it easier to compare quality, cost and risk. It also notes that interoperability lowers the cost of changing parts of an AI application. The New Stack piece makes a similar argument, stressing that interoperability is what will decide which AI observability approaches succeed. Both articles treat common data formats as the practical requirement for teams that want to swap components without rebuilding their monitoring.

Both articles point to specific practices and tools. TechGig cites OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, which describe common concepts for conversations and messages and allow large content to be stored externally with references kept in telemetry, and it names Splunk's Agent Observability work, built on OpenTelemetry and AGNTCY standards, as one vendor-neutral example. It also quotes the argument that cost per business outcome is more useful than cost per token, since token counts alone do not show whether spending produced useful work. The New Stack article, which is largely a discussion of interoperability as the central contest in the field, is framed around the same idea that open standards will shape the market. The pieces were published by technology news outlets and attribute these views to the authors and the cited vendors rather than to any regulator.

What happens next is not spelled out in detail by either article. TechGig suggests that agent observability can support guardrails that block harmful actions when connected to enforcement systems, and that shared telemetry can link those controls to evidence about an agent's steps and business impact. The New Stack article predicts that the AI observability race will be decided by interoperability, but it does not give a timeline or specific milestones. The reporting therefore describes a direction of travel toward shared standards and measurable business value, while leaving open how quickly organisations will adopt them.

stories.Headline: States Don’t Have to Solve the AI Education Equation Alone. Tennessee Shows How
stories.Summary:
States across the country are taking different approaches to AI policy, with governors forming task forces, state education agencies issuing non-binding guidance, and legislatures requiring districts to adopt AI policies. A November 2025 survey found that 93% of 29 state education agency respondents had communicated or planned to communicate a vision for AI in K-12 education, but only 43% had assisted or planned to assist districts with implementation support. Among the 39 states and territories studied for a state early adopter database, just 11% had reached the "integrator" stage of moving past guidance into pilots, evaluation, procurement help, and implementation strategies. The authors, Bree Dusseault and Dana Harrison of the Center on Reinventing Public Education, argue that this gap leaves schools without the practical help they need. The authors say AI is a difficult policy area because both the technology and public opinion change quickly, so guidance and task forces alone fall short.

School and district leaders need state help with vetting products, generating evidence on what works, and building trust in how AI is used. States also need infrastructure that links policy to classroom practice and turns scattered local experiments into shared knowledge. The article notes that many state education agencies lack the funding or internal expertise to lead these efforts. Intermediary organizations, the authors write, can fill that role, and a majority of participants in their study reported pursuing partnerships for strategy development, implementation, or both.

The article uses Tennessee's State Collaborative on Reforming Education, known as SCORE, as its main example. SCORE is a statewide nonprofit without formal authority over district decisions, and its influence comes from long-standing relationships with state leaders, districts, colleges, funders, and technology providers. After Tennessee required districts to adopt AI policies covering safety, academic integrity, and risk mitigation, SCORE convened a working group that met regularly for roughly 18 months, and its recommendations were reflected in the state's Action Plan. SCORE also helps districts evaluate tools without endorsing products, and it helped fund a larger rollout of Coursemojo, an AI-enabled literacy tool, across seven districts, 20 schools, and more than 4,000 students in 2025-26.

The authors say participating leaders and teachers reported positive results, and districts later renewed the work, often with their own funds. The authors stress that the Tennessee model need not be copied exactly, since an intermediary could be a nonprofit, a university, a technical service provider, or a research group, as long as it has trust, staying power, and the ability to connect people who do not normally work together. They warn that without such coordinated support, better-resourced districts may experiment while smaller and higher-need systems struggle to evaluate tools, set safeguards, and provide training, which could widen existing inequities. They conclude that the next phase of state AI leadership will depend less on publishing guidance than on building infrastructure for continuous learning, so that policies set direction and partnerships provide the capacity to follow it.

stories.Headline: UnitedHealthcare Is Rolling Out Its AI Agent To 21 Million Members
stories.Summary:
UnitedHealthcare is expanding access to Avery, its generative AI companion designed to support care coordination for members, to 21 million people. The tool was first unveiled earlier this year, when it was available to about 6.5 million members in employer plans and 160,000 people enrolled in Medicare Advantage. The expansion is growing the tool's reach faster than the insurer originally expected, according to the reporting. The company says Avery has resolved 90% of member interactions, and in the remaining 10% of cases it can hand off to a human advocate.

Avery is built on what the company calls ground truth systems, a data foundation that sits on top of the information available through UnitedHealthcare. Craig Kurtzweil, the company's chief data and analytics officer, said that foundation is what lets members get better answers. Avery can provide details on deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, provider networks, pricing and claims processing. Kurtzweil said accuracy is central to members trusting the tool and using it effectively. He described making the tool as accurate as possible as a major part of earning consumers' trust.

Kurtzweil told Fierce Healthcare that the expansion makes sense given the early results and feedback from users. He said Avery fits into a broader push to put more information in members' hands, including plan designs like Surest, which offer variable copayments that let members choose providers and care. The team is also building an option for Avery to call providers and schedule appointments on a member's behalf. Kurtzweil said the company intends to keep widening access until all of its enrollees can use the tool. He added that more and more people will be affected as the company works to reduce friction and make things easier for consumers.

Cloud-native AI agent harnesses and Kubernetes GPU optimisation are drawing attention across the cloud infrastructure sector. The articles do not name a single party responsible for setting industry direction, and the claims about Koordinator's results come from a single case study reported in the coverage.

On October 27, 2026, South Korea's benchmark Kospi index rose 3.09 percent to close at 5,638.34 points, driven by gains in technology shares and renewed optimism about artificial intelligence. The Korea Exchange activated a buy-side sidecar at 10:13 a.m., halting buy orders in program trading for five minutes, the first such action in four trading sessions. Trading was light, with 183.13 million shares changing hands worth 15.29 trillion won, and advancing stocks outnumbered decliners 593 to 274. Foreign and institutional investors were net buyers while individual investors sold heavily. The Korea Exchange's sidecar rule is triggered when Kospi 200 futures rise at least 5 percent and stay at that level for one minute or longer.

The rally followed an overnight rise on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite climbed 0.82 percent. Investor enthusiasm for AI-related stocks was reignited after Anthropic disclosed strong revenue growth in its U.S. initial public offering filing. Oil prices also fell on hopes of easing Middle East tensions, following reports of Qatari mediation involving Iran and the United States. Samsung Electronics rose 4.23 percent to 222,000 won, while SK hynix climbed 5.18 percent to 1.34 million won. The won weakened 0.6 won against the dollar to trade at 1,323.7 as of 3:30 p.m.

Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities, said that foreign and institutional investors bought major semiconductor stocks because of renewed interest in AI, despite lingering macroeconomic concerns. Bond prices closed higher, with the yield on three-year Treasurys falling 3.1 basis points to 3.758 and the return on five-year government bonds dropping 3.3 basis points to 3.899. Separately, a report released on October 26 by Samil PwC, the South Korean member firm of the global consultancy, warned local chipmakers to defend their profitability. The firm said Chinese competition would likely intensify first in conventional memory, mature-node manufacturing, and packaging and testing. It urged Samsung and SK hynix to sharpen cost competitiveness in commodity memory while expanding into advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, which is used alongside AI processors.

stories.Headline: GDPR and CRM: What your customer data obligations mean
stories.Summary:
Article 1, published by HubSpot on October 27, 2026, explains how the EU General Data Protection Regulation applies to customer data kept in a CRM system. It says GDPR covers any CRM record holding personal data about people in the European Union or United Kingdom, wherever the company is based. The guide notes that this includes contact details, form submissions, emails, call logs, and behavioral data such as email opens. It stresses that a company must identify and document a lawful basis before processing that data, with consent and legitimate interest being the two bases that come up most often in CRM work. The article recommends tracking the lawful basis for each record separately rather than applying one setting to every contact.

The article describes what the rules require in practice. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, so a pre-checked box or silence does not count, and subscription preferences should be granular so a person can opt out of marketing emails without opting out of other communications. Individuals hold rights of access, rectification, portability, restriction, erasure, and objection, and the article says each needs a repeatable process rather than an ad hoc response. For erasure, it warns that deleting a record from the core CRM is not enough if connected tools still hold it, since the data can resurface on the next sync. Objections to direct marketing must be honored immediately, and the objection itself should be logged so the status is not lost.

The article also addresses data minimization and retention, advising teams to collect only fields with a stated purpose and to review retention on a quarterly or biannual cadence. The article is written by Sam Lauron and presented as a guide from HubSpot, which sells CRM software and describes its own features as supporting compliant execution. It states that these features help with compliance but do not guarantee it, and it advises organizations to work with a legal advisor or data privacy expert. The article does not report any enforcement action or specific incident. It is a general explanation of obligations, and it does not indicate any further steps beyond what teams should do to set up their own processes.

Article 2, published by BusinessWorld Online on October 26, 2026, is the second part of a piece on how boards should govern data and artificial intelligence. It sets out several themes, including maintaining an inventory of reports, models, generative AI uses, and agents with assigned owners, and tiering controls by potential impact in line with risk-based approaches such as ISO 31000. It urges clear accountability, ongoing monitoring across the full life cycle, and treating vendors as part of the control environment. It also distinguishes binding law, such as the Data Privacy Act of 2012, from supervisory guidance and voluntary frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and it says personal data must be processed lawfully before it enters any model. The piece suggests that board committees can divide oversight among risk, audit, and governance matters while the full board keeps accountability, and it closes with questions directors should ask management.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT’s expanding world of work
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a new dataset on October 26, 2026, called OpenAI Signals data, which shows how people use ChatGPT for work across nearly 100 countries. The data covers 165 work activities, from preparing instructional materials and developing marketing content to programming and analyzing business data. It is organized quarterly from the first quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026. The release is meant to give researchers a new way to study AI's role in the economy.

The data is built on O*NET, a standardized framework that groups occupation-specific tasks into broader work activities shared across jobs. This shared structure lets researchers compare ChatGPT use with other occupational and employment data. The dataset shows wide variation across countries, and work-related use has become less concentrated in the most common activities over time. Across 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common activities made up an average of 51.1% of classified work messages in Q3 2026, down from 56.0% in Q1 2025. The data covers work-related messages on individual ChatGPT plans and excludes enterprise messages and Codex use.

OpenAI published the release under its Economic Research team and says it is part of its ongoing OpenAI Signals effort to share evidence about how people use AI. The company states that researchers do not read individual conversations, since automated systems classify messages after identifying information is removed. Results are published only in aggregate, small groups are withheld, and statistical noise is added to protect individual messages. OpenAI invites researchers to explore the data, connect it with other sources, and examine what these patterns mean for workers and businesses.

Separately, on October 23, 2026, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella said in his annual letter that the company is building a broader AI ecosystem while reducing the cost of AI-powered services. Nadella argued that customers will increasingly measure the cost of tokens against the outcomes they produce, which he called the "cost-to-outcome" frontier. He said Microsoft is accelerating capacity deployment and improving efficiency across its infrastructure, and reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $331.8 billion, up 18 per cent. He also noted that Azure grew 41 per cent and that Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, with the company stressing that AI's benefits should be shared broadly.

stories.Headline: Lumion Highlights AI Agents for After-Hours Inquiries and Lead Follow-Up
stories.Summary:
Lumion, a technology company based in Salt Lake City, Utah, announced on October 27, 2026 that it is promoting AI agents built to handle customer inquiries, automated follow-up, and outreach to prospective customers. The platform combines AI-powered communication, workflow automation, and a unified inbox so organizations can manage calls, text messages, and website inquiries in one place. The company says the agents answer after-hours calls and other messages around the clock, and they can capture conversation details for employees to review later. The announcement targets a familiar problem, namely that inquiries often arrive when staff cannot respond, and delayed replies can cause prospects to move on.

The agents are meant to handle routine questions and record relevant context while leaving employees free to take over conversations that need more attention. A unified inbox gathers interactions from phone, email, and text so staff do not have to check several systems to see a customer's history. The platform also includes lead reactivation, which lets businesses reconnect with older prospects who never enrolled or completed a transaction. Lumion says businesses can start using the agents in as little as two weeks, configured around each organization's information and processes. Afterward, customers can extend the platform into application and onboarding workflows.

Lumion's chief statements come from Bilal Aslim, who is quoted in the announcement. He says a customer inquiry can arrive at any time, while a business team cannot always respond right away. According to Aslim, AI agents can help maintain continuity by responding to initial inquiries, capturing context, and supporting follow-up, so employees can concentrate on work that needs their judgment. The company presents the platform as a way to coordinate these tasks rather than to remove people from customer communication.

The announcement includes one customer example. At a career school, AI outreach to leads inactive for about two years produced two enrollments in the first week and 14 more over the following several weeks, with the first two generating a combined $10,000 in paid deposits. The articles stress that this reflects one customer's experience and that other organizations may see different results depending on lead quality and prospect responses. The company also says it has worked with more than 400 businesses and has managed and generated over $300 million in customer revenue through its platform. It further reports a $10.7 million seed round announced June 16, 2025, led by TTV Capital with participation from Tusk Venture Partners, intended to support market expansion and product innovation.

stories.Headline: Cadence unveils Nvidia-backed AI models that chipmakers can run in-house - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Cadence Design Systems on Monday, October 26, 2026, launched a portfolio of AI models tuned for chip design, called Cadence Maestro. The company built the suite in part on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and secured it with Nvidia's OpenShell safety technology, deepening a partnership between the two firms. Cadence and rival Synopsys both make software used to arrange billions of transistors to meet cost and performance targets, and both are racing to have AI agents use those tools for human engineers. The Next Platform reported that the models were fine-tuned on Nvidia's Nemotron family to work with and interpret results from Cadence's own tools. Cadence has also rolled out a series of agent products over the past year, including AuraStack, ChipStack, InnoStack and ViraStack.

Customers can run the Maestro models on Cadence's own cloud or any public cloud, or keep them entirely in-house behind their own firewalls and data centers. They can also fine-tune the models on their own chip designs, though Paul Cunningham told The Next Platform that this would be offered more as a managed service than something customers set up alone. Cadence says early results show up to 30% higher quality and up to five times better cost-efficiency compared with general-purpose models. The first Maestro models will reach select early-access customers in the fourth quarter. Access can also come through an API or a secure virtual private cloud, or on premises for those with the necessary hardware.

Cunningham, a senior vice president at Cadence, framed Maestro as model-agnostic, noting that there are more AI model providers than chip design software vendors. Asked whether Cadence might strike deals with proprietary AI labs, he said open-weight and closed-weight approaches are being pursued equally, and that working with commercial labs is part of the Maestro vision, though he declined to elaborate. He also said that somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development today are being designed with help from AI agents, and that the share is growing rapidly. On the limits of general models, he said powerful off-the-shelf foundation models are a starting point and can still be specialized.

The launch contrasts with the approach of Synopsys, Cadence's largest competitor, which said on September 30 that it would develop an AI model with OpenAI and share revenue with the ChatGPT maker. That model, GPT-Synopsys, will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure. The Next Platform noted that Cadence's earlier agents were largely powered by off-the-shelf language models, which had limited exposure to design formats such as RTL, and that the new models aim to fix that gap. It added that Nvidia has been pushing high-performance computing and AI together for years, a trend also reflected in the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission.

stories.Headline: ‘If you’re hungry in the city, this building’s for you,’ Met Council says of new, $25 million, AI-powered Brooklyn warehouse

The Met Council, a Jewish anti-poverty organization, opened a new $25 million, AI-powered food distribution warehouse in Canarsie, Brooklyn, on Monday, October 26, 2026. The 22,000-square-foot facility lets people in need order groceries in advance for home delivery or pickup, instead of taking whatever is available at a pantry. Roughly 250 people attended the opening, which the organization called the largest capital project in its history. The warehouse was built to serve up to a million people a year, and the group hopes to eventually triple its current reach beyond the more than 350,000 New Yorkers it serves annually.

The facility uses advanced cold storage, automation and artificial intelligence to manage inventory and distribute food more efficiently. It supports the Met Council's network of more than 200 food pantry partners across the five boroughs, along with year-round kosher and halal distributions. It also helps the group provide medically tailored meals and groceries to eligible Medicaid recipients through New York's Social Care Network program. Officials described the project as a major step in expanding the group's ability to feed hungry New Yorkers. The building was reported to have taken about five years to develop.

David Greenfield, the Met Council's chief executive, said the organization was building infrastructure to fight poverty on a much larger scale, and he called the project a labor of love. He told attendees that anyone who is hungry in the city is welcome at the building, regardless of background or language. Joseph Allerhand, the group's co-president, said the facility shows its commitment to feeding those who need help most, including working-class and middle-class families. Speakers at the event, including New York City Comptroller Mark Levine and state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, praised the use of technology to reduce waste and serve more people.

The project sits within growing demand for food assistance across the city, and speakers linked the work to public safety and community strength. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said his own family needed help to get by and that such support can strengthen neighborhoods. Greenfield closed by citing a Torah commandment to care for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, saying an open hand is open to everyone. stories.Headline: Apple announces Siri AI will expand to these new languages soon
stories.Summary:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on Monday, October 26, 2026, as the first major updates to the iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 systems that launched in September. The update expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, which were not supported before, and it adds several other features. Apple also said four more languages, Chinese (Traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, will arrive by the end of the year. Siri AI was previously available only in English.

The Siri AI improvements in this release let the assistant recall earlier conversations, so a user can ask about a restaurant it suggested the week before. It can also draw on more sources, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, voicemails, and Safari history and Reading List. A new Excluded Apps setting lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can reach from one place. Other additions include Messages suggestions that help with tasks like adding a dinner invite to Calendar, and support for SynthID watermarking in Photos and Image Playground. The update also brings Simple Profiles to the Apple TV app and lets FaceTime calls include a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner.

Apple did not describe who was responsible for the changes beyond the company itself, and the articles give no statement from any individual. The release notes say Siri AI is not available in the European Union or mainland China. Bloomberg reporting cited in one article says Apple plans to bring some initial Apple Intelligence features to China with iOS 27.3, but Siri AI is not expected among them. The articles expect the new Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese support to arrive with iOS 27.3, which is expected in December, with its first beta possibly appearing the following week.

The release also comes alongside other Apple announcements, including a new Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI announced on October 13. Users can get the update by going to Settings, then General, then Software Update. Apple also released iOS 26.7.2 with security fixes. Readers who have tried Siri AI in a language other than English have been invited to share their experiences in the comments.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI Foundation expands with four new projects
stories.Summary:
The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has grown from three projects to ten in its first year, adding four new initiatives at the AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 event in San Jose on October 22 and 23. Mazin Gilbert, the foundation's executive director, announced the new projects along with three new governance committees. Alibaba contributed OpenSandbox, a secure sandbox for running agents, while OpenAI contributed Open Responses, a specification for interoperable large language model interfaces. Anthropic added its Agent Skills standard, and Hugging Face contributed OpenEnv, a framework for reinforcement learning environments. The event itself shifted much of its focus toward protocol features, security, and identity.

Open Responses already has support from AWS Bedrock, Databricks, Ollama, Nvidia, and vLLM, according to coverage of the event. Anthropic's Model Context Protocol received a stateless server mode in its July 28 specification, and about 70 percent of traffic on some platforms already uses it. Anthropic also announced support for MCP tasks in Claude Code, which lets tool calls run for minutes, hours, or even days. On the security side, cumulative SDK downloads for the protocol have reached 4.17 billion, up from about 3 billion a month earlier. About a third of the 116 conformance scenarios now test security, and enterprise-managed authorization is live in Claude.

Manik Surtani, the foundation's CTO, said the organization launched a year ago with a belief that agentic AI needed a neutral home to thrive. He compared the situation to Kubernetes, which succeeded after Google moved it into a neutral foundation. Surtani argued that a license alone does not keep infrastructure open and said the remaining open problems sit in identity, attestation, audit, and payments. Some outside observers were more skeptical, with one publication noting that Anthropic still defines its own Messages API and Google its Interactions API. Another warned that the rapid embrace of AI agents may be too fast for some industries.

Other speakers addressed practical and security concerns. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor, warned that frontier AI could help attackers more than defenders in the near term, citing a benchmark in which one model produced about 230 working exploits against 869 targets in two hours. Her proposed response was secure-by-construction systems supported by AI-generated proofs. Chrome's Sarah Drasner presented WebMCP, a proposed web standard in origin trial that lets websites expose tools directly to agents, which she said can make some actions 2.5 to 7.5 times faster and complements MCP rather than replacing it. Block also demonstrated Buzz, an open source workspace where people and agents share channels, with version 1.0 expected in mid-November.

stories.Headline: KT takes on global cloud providers with new enterprise AI service
stories.Summary:
KT, the South Korean telecom company, unveiled an enterprise AI platform called Token Factory on Tuesday that lets businesses use models from different providers through a single service. The platform launches Friday with 73 models, and KT plans to expand that lineup to more than 500 in November through a partnership with OpenRouter, a US-based AI marketplace. The move is aimed at global cloud operators such as Amazon and Microsoft. KT said the idea grew out of problems its corporate clients raised, including the desire to adopt newer models without overhauling their systems and to keep employee AI use within company security controls.

Through Token Factory, customers can choose models, monitor their usage, and pay in Korean won, with charges that can be combined with existing telecom bills. An automated system sends simpler requests to cheaper models and harder tasks to higher-performance ones. KT estimates this could cut AI processing costs by up to 25 percent, though it has not disclosed the criteria behind its internal tests. Kim Jun-seok, head of KT's Agentic AI Lab, attributed about 20 percent of the savings to removing unnecessary text from prompts and about 5 percent to choosing the least expensive capable model. Larger customers will also be offered volume discounts and dedicated network options.

OpenRouter provides access to models from developers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and the partnership could also let KT sell services hosted in Korea to overseas customers. OpenRouter's founder and CEO, Alex Atallah, said in a recorded message that the tie-up extends model choice to Korean enterprises with the option of using infrastructure located in Korea. OpenRouter agreed in August to be acquired by the US payments company Stripe in a deal reportedly worth more than $8 billion. Lee Jin-hyoung, head of KT's AX business unit, said marketplace commissions of around 5 percent are not KT's main business, which instead centers on running models on its own GPUs.

KT has not released detailed prices for its seven locally hosted models, though it expects them to cost less than comparable services and says domestic processing may appeal to banks and public institutions with strict data requirements. Only seven of the 73 launch models will run in KT's Korean data centers, and most models supplied through OpenRouter will process requests overseas. The company has not disclosed revenue targets or confirmed how many paying customers it has. The article's context also includes a separate release from One Stop Systems, a US maker of high-performance computing hardware, which said on October 26 that its Gen5 4UP-MAX expansion system has been qualified for use with a tier 1 global enterprise computing platform provider.

stories.Headline: EXCLUSIVE: US political candidates tailor messages for AI models used by voters
stories.Summary:
US political candidates have been shaping their campaign messages to appeal to AI chatbots that more voters now consult on issues, according to documents seen by Reuters and reported on October 26, 2026. One PowerPoint presentation laid out a plan for Mike Minogue, the Republican challenger to Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey, to persuade chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to present him as the preferred choice on key issues. The strategy went well beyond traditional search engine optimization, aiming instead to control what AI systems say when voters ask about taxes, housing and public safety. The plan would involve creating hundreds of AI-friendly policy pages, placing paid content on websites that chatbots often cite, and tracking chatbot answers so the content could be adjusted until responses matched the candidate's platform. The presentation described this approach as generative engine optimization, or GEO.

The firm behind the document, Visigent of Austin, Texas, said fees for such work vary widely. CEO Thomas Howell said political clients start at about $5,000 a month, and could reach $50,000 a month if paid media and influencer outreach are added. Visigent's website lists software at $134 a month and up to $9,000 monthly for large clients needing editorial design and development. The presentation also shows a top success fee of $200,000 for a "category win." Howell said these fees are expected to rise as the 2028 presidential cycle begins after the midterm elections.

A separate option, CampSight, operated by the Run for Something Action Fund, charges campaigns between $9 and $250 per month and offers custom pricing for statewide and federal races. Joe Bonilla, managing partner of the New York firm Relentless Awareness, said campaigns using AI influence training will be widespread by the 2028 cycle, which will include a presidential election. He also said the public increasingly cannot tell content created by systems like Claude and ChatGPT apart from human-written material. Cameron Hickey, CEO of the National Conference on Citizenship, said about 25% of eligible voters have asked a chatbot about a political candidate when deciding how to vote. Meg Schwenzfeier of Caucus AI warned that chatbots can speak with great confidence while drawing on large amounts of unvetted information, so safeguards against misinformation are needed.

The Minogue campaign did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters reported that the practice is still new, and experts disagree about its risks. Jordan Haines, chief technology officer at Run for Something, said his group had seen Reddit posts appear in AI answers within a day, but that this concern had not fully materialized, as chatbots appeared to separate reputable information from unreliable sources. The reporting does not say whether any regulation or disclosure rule applies to such campaign efforts. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tsinghua University & NVIDIA Unveil New AI Video Model Ranking: Exposing Shortcomings of 38 Real-Time Generative AI Video Systems
stories.Summary:
Tsinghua University, NVIDIA and several other universities and research institutions have jointly released StreamEval, a new benchmark for streaming interactive AI video generation. The ranking covers 38 models, and the researchers presented it in late October 2026 as the first evaluation of its kind in the industry. Existing tools such as VBench and EvalCrafter judge a single prompt and the video it produces, which leaves them unable to test how these systems handle instructions that keep arriving during generation. StreamEval was built to close that gap by testing the systems under conditions closer to real use.

The benchmark spans five task types: digital human dialogue, virtual human performance, world generation, instruction editing and reference editing. Each type has 60 test cases, run at durations of 15, 30, 60, 120 and 300 seconds, and each case is run three times by the same model. The full dataset includes 1,347 online events released step by step along the timeline, so a model sees only the input available at that moment. Performance is scored across four dimensions and ten indicators, each rated from 0 to 100, and the five task types are ranked separately rather than merged into one overall list. All code, datasets and scoring rules are open source, and developers can submit their own models to the leaderboard.

The results show that a model producing stable video does not necessarily follow changing instructions. In digital human dialogue, Vidu S2-Avatar reached the top overall score among participating models that support custom images, at 93.98 after a 5-point bonus. In virtual human performance, the same system scored highest overall at 81.71, yet its instruction-following score was only 36.90, the highest value among seven models but still low. In world generation, the top overall scores were held by different models on different measures, which the researchers say shows that visual quality, instruction response and long-term continuity must be judged separately. The reference editing task was the hardest, with the best overall score at 39.02 and an edit success rate of only 15.00.

A separate report from the same period describes Cadence Design Systems and NVIDIA announcing a partnership and the Maestro AI model family, fine-tuned on NVIDIA's Nemotron models to work with Cadence's electronic design automation tools. Cadence's Paul Cunningham said that somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development are now designed with help from AI agents, a share he expects to keep growing. Cadence claims early testing showed up to a 30 percent gain in output quality and up to five times better token efficiency compared with general-purpose foundation models. The Maestro platform can be accessed through an API, run in a secure virtual private cloud, or deployed on premises, with customization on customer data offered as a managed service. The same report links this trend to the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which has driven a series of new Nvidia-based supercomputers.

stories.Headline: Korea should not sacrifice AI boom over chip dependence fears: IDB economist
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Laura Alfaro, chief economist and economic counselor at the Inter-American Development Bank, told a press conference in Seoul that Korea should keep pursuing the artificial intelligence boom rather than slow growth out of worry about its heavy reliance on semiconductors. She made the remarks at the Global Financial Stability Conference 2026, hosted by the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Korea Development Institute. Her position was that the country should instead cushion itself against swings through stabilization funds and greater structural flexibility. The comments were reported by the Korea Times and the JoongAng Daily, the latter with a wire contribution from Yonhap.

Alfaro compared Korea's exposure to chips with the "resource curse" that has affected Latin America, where economies dependent on minerals and oil suffer when commodity prices fluctuate sharply. To manage such cycles, she recommended a stabilization fund that would set aside part of the gains made during boom periods and draw on them during downturns. Such a fund could also limit excessive appreciation of the domestic currency and soften the effects of large, rapid capital inflows. She also called for more flexibility in labor markets and government spending, saying the core problem in boom-and-bust cycles is an inability to adjust in downturns. The JoongAng Daily reported that Korea has proposed a Future Fund, drawing on sources including windfall tax revenue from chipmakers, with a general account and four program accounts covering youth, growth engines, regional development, and education and talent development.

Alfaro said she was not familiar with the details of the government's proposed Future Response Fund but supported its underlying rationale, and the JoongAng Daily quoted her as saying the "spirit" of the Future Fund sounds like what needs to be done. Asked whether debt repayment should take priority over building assets, she said neither approach was necessarily superior, since both amount to saving. She also described herself as "AI positive" and argued that concern over volatility should not deter investment in the technology, since productivity gains from AI offer a route to growth in a region facing shrinking birth rates. Separately, she said Latin America's green energy and mineral resources, such as copper, could support mutually beneficial exchange with Korea in AI, given how energy-intensive the technology is. The reports do not indicate any formal government response to these remarks or what steps will follow.

stories.Headline: An Anthropic hiring manager says he stopped giving coding interviews because Claude is better at them and tells junior engineers that "hunger beats tenure" (Felix Rieseberg)
stories.Summary:
An Anthropic hiring manager, Felix Rieseberg, has announced that he has stopped giving the traditional coding interview to candidates, saying Claude now outperforms people on those tests. He wrote about the decision in a post dated October 27, 2026, saying the change happened "this month." He once found small coding challenges useful for predicting how well a candidate would do on his teams, but he says that is no longer true. He also says his most impactful builders succeed regardless of how well they perform on these tests.

He argues that the change matters most for engineers without social capital, status, or power, whom he describes as a group that includes junior developers. Rather than seeing AI purely as a threat to newcomers, he says that impact now depends less on years of accumulated knowledge of frameworks and libraries. He writes that engineers who are comparatively new are outpacing people who are probably better coders and have been around longer. His summary of this idea is that hunger beats tenure. He sees fresh eyes as an advantage, since newcomers can notice friction and opportunities that longtime employees have stopped seeing.

He offers several steps for these engineers. He advises them to focus on business impact over the backlog, to pick one ambitious idea, and to build a working prototype over a weekend instead of relying on lengthy product documents and lobbying. He cautions against cramming several ideas into one prototype, since that can hide the strongest one. He also suggests using a fresh perspective, especially for user-facing products, where newcomers may empathize with outside users more easily. He points to Anthropic's Claude Code, whose first public version, he says, was built by two relatively new engineers over one weekend and shipped about eight days later.

He is not the only manager working out how to hire for AI-assisted building, and he says he is now scanning resumes and portfolios for small prototypes that show taste, empathy, and principled thinking. He does not say what will replace the coding interview in full, and he invites others to share better approaches. He is also optimistic that promotion by tenure will matter less over time. He frames his view as a personal assessment grounded in what he has seen at Anthropic, Stripe, Notion, and Slack, not as a settled industry standard.

Fierce Healthcare reported that Optum Ventures took part as well. The platform is free for licensed clinicians and medical trainees, who can ask questions about diagnoses, medication dosing, guidelines and treatment and receive summaries linked to their sources.

The company plans to use the new capital to improve its platform, scale into more healthcare markets and expand partnerships with medical societies, publishers and health systems. It also intends to keep investing in locally relevant clinical guidance and in tools that let healthcare institutions add their own medical knowledge to the platform through its Vera Spaces offering. Fierce Healthcare reported that the platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and drug labels, and that it is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from a few thousand a year earlier. The company also said it doubled its team from six to 12 people and is now hiring internationally.

Taieb Bennani, a cofounder of Vera Health, has described the company's focus on clinicians and its emphasis on evidence. He said clinicians make decisions in seconds and that the team, which includes clinicians or their relatives, builds the product around that need. Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner Emily Melton said in a statement that the platform starts with evidence rather than just an answer, which helps clinicians assess the research behind a decision. Bennani also told Fierce Healthcare that the company's approach rests on honesty, traceability, transparency and context, and that the tool searches for evidence before writing an answer.

The funding comes amid growing competition in clinical AI search. MobiHealthNews noted that OpenEvidence secured $250 million in Series D funding in January, doubling its valuation to $12 billion, and that Doximity recently partnered with Wolters Kluwer Health to bring UpToDate content into its Ask tool. Fierce Healthcare added that established reference companies such as Elsevier's ClinicalKey and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate are competing with AI-native tools as well as consumer technology firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. stories.Headline: Police Are Using AI to Pull Over Drivers for 'Suspicious' Behavior
stories.Summary:
Police in several U.S. states are using automated license plate readers and AI-powered tools to flag drivers for "suspicious" travel patterns, even when those drivers are not suspected of a specific crime. The American Civil Liberties Union raised the alarm in an October 2026 post, opening with the case of Grace Knowles, a woman from northern Virginia who was pulled over in September 2025 while driving from New Orleans toward Florida. An officer told her he had been left-lane driving, then said he was an FBI special agent and that her plate had been flagged for suspicious travel patterns. He showed her a computer map with circles marking where her car had been, each linked to a photo of her license plate. Knowles said he told her the cameras were everywhere, including on top of highway signs.

The ACLU warns that such stops could become more common as companies such as Flock Safety and Axon sell systems that scan plates as vehicles pass and record each car's time and location. Police can search that data during investigations, and privacy advocates note that it captures millions of people who are not suspected of any crime, often without a warrant. Flock has reportedly developed an AI tool that can identify and track vehicles by movement patterns alone, and records describe queries that combine plate reads with arrest records and commercial data broker files. Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ACLU says the trend is spreading and points to pretextual stops, in which drivers are pulled over for minor or invented violations as cover for the real reason.

Responsibility here rests with the police agencies using these tools and with the vendors that build and sell them, and the articles describe them as operating under little legal limit. Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU, wrote that for many people these encounters will be far more frightening and dangerous than what Knowles experienced. The ACLU is pressing for limits on this kind of surveillance. A federal jury in Texas recently sided with a man who sued over what his attorneys called an unconstitutional traffic stop scheme based on license plate readers, and the case is a sign that courts may be willing to examine these practices.

Public opinion is divided, with an August YouGov survey finding that 46% of respondents opposed police use of the technology in their communities and 38% supported it. Several agencies, including the Los Angeles Police Department, have suspended or ended their Flock contracts amid the backlash. Other reported cases include a California grandmother questioned by Customs and Border Protection about her casino visits and a man stopped repeatedly after driving between Wisconsin and Michigan. As the systems expand, the articles suggest that more stops of this kind are likely, though how courts and lawmakers will respond remains unsettled.

stories.Headline: AI-generated models spark job fears and image rights battle in fashion world
stories.Summary:
AI-generated models are raising alarm across the fashion industry after a Reuters investigation found that brands are seeking broad rights over models' images. Reuters interviewed 15 modelling agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential contracts from brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal. The draft terms asked for permission to swap model faces using AI, to create digital clones without extra pay, and to use body images to train AI tools. Many of the agreements also contained broad legal wording that would give brands wide discretion over how the technology is used.

The shift matters because AI can cut production costs by more than 90 per cent compared with traditional photo shoots. Agencies report falling bookings and some studios have closed, with e-commerce work for fast-fashion platforms, a key source of income for models, under particular pressure. London-based model Adot Gak warned that the industry could soon be dominated by bots if models do not speak up. Fast-fashion brands such as Mango have already adopted computer-generated models at scale, while luxury houses have moved more cautiously. Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models on its website or in promotional material.

Several companies responded to the findings, though not all gave the same account. Diesel's parent company, OTB, said the casting sheet was drafted for one campaign and does not reflect its standard contracts. Calvin Klein said it is testing and learning in a fast-moving space and that its use of AI follows regulations and respects the rights of its models. L'Oreal did not comment directly on the clause about altering product appearance but said it uses standard AI tools in post-production that leave model likenesses unaffected. Reale Actives said it hires real talent and blamed the contract language on a third-party production partner.

Legal protections remain uneven, and the New York State Fashion Workers Act is described as a notable exception. From June 2025, that law bars companies from generating or modifying model replicas without explicit consent. Sara Ziff of the Model Alliance is pushing for similar protections in other US states and at the federal level. In Britain, the British Fashion Model Agents Association has issued an AI code of practice requiring explicit consent, but its head, John Horner, warned that without binding rules, models remain exposed. Industry voices say young models may not grasp how long signed AI rights could affect their careers.

Bashirli said the centre would help build human capital, strengthen the country's economic competitiveness and raise its innovation potential. stories.Headline: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Monday, October 26, 2026 three results in mathematics, computer science and physics, along with a stated new approach to sharing its findings. The announcement followed a turbulent few months in which the company released hundreds of AI-generated preprints on mathematicians at the start of October. This time, OpenAI said it would work with expert "shepherds" to decide how to share the work, and each result got a different release strategy. The mathematics output was released as AI-generated text, leaving researchers to organize their own explanations, the computer science finding will be explained by an outside group of researchers, and the physics result has not been released at all, with OpenAI deferring to outside experts on how to proceed.

The mathematics result claims to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions, a question about how little space is needed to turn a needle in every direction. Brown University mathematician Brendan Hassett said the claim "looks well supported," though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization used to verify it computationally. The physics result concerns quantum chromodynamics and its link to Yang-Mills theory, but it does not address the unresolved mass gap in the related Millennium Prize problem. The computer science result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption that closely relates to the P versus NP question. Researchers described the results as huge, major and significant, though they noted the difficulty of checking them.

Researchers who spoke to The Verge said they were tired of OpenAI's conduct, and many objected to handpicking experts to review the work first. Constantin Kogler of the Institute for Advanced Study said it made no sense for only a few scientists to see the results first, while Andreas Karch of the University of Texas at Austin called the handpicked group a disaster and asked why the proof could not be released publicly now. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence had warned a day earlier against this practice, recommending release on scholarly repositories with formal proofs and funding for independent work. After the announcement, that group urged OpenAI to publish the physics output without delay, arguing the Lean formalization was already complete. Xiaoyu He of Georgia Institute of Technology said the deeper concern is that fundamental results are arriving quickly without human contribution and are hard to read and verify, a problem that changes in release method cannot fix.

stories.Headline: Trump wants everyone to stop saying "AI."
stories.Summary:
Trump has said he wants to stop people from using the term "AI." In a Truth Social post dated October 27, 2026, he wrote that he would soon be officially banning the phrase "AI/Artificial Intelligence" in all relevant documents and everything else, citing its inaccuracy. He had earlier asked when The Wall Street Journal would swap the term for "Super Intelligence." The post was reported by The Verge. The change he described would apply legally only to executive branch agencies, so it would not bind private companies, the press or the public.

A widely shared screenshot of the post accompanied the coverage. The announcement is a notable example of a head of state weighing in on the naming of a technology rather than on its regulation. Reporting on the post mostly framed it as a question of terminology and its legal reach. Separately, Lim Woong, a professor at the Graduate School of Education at Yonsei University, wrote a column in The Korea Herald published October 27, 2026, criticizing a different political episode. President Lee Jae Myung had posted on social media an exchange with Gemini, Google's generative AI, to rebut critics of having top investigators and prosecutors attend his Cabinet meetings.

Lim argued that a chatbot's answer depends heavily on how a question is framed, so it should not settle a constitutional debate. He said the president's approach invited ridicule and that the opposition had responded with an "I asked AI, too" challenge. Lim's column went beyond that episode and offered a list of phrases he said thoughtful people should stop using, such as "I asked AI, and it says so." He argued that such remarks hand off agency and accountability that belong to people, and he urged institutions like schools, courts and newsrooms to be clear about where machine output ends and human judgment begins. The Korea Herald presented the piece as the writer's own opinion, not an official position.

stories.Headline: South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
South Korea's economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter, driven by strong global demand for chips used in artificial intelligence. Gross domestic product expanded 1 percent from the previous quarter, or 3.4 percent from a year earlier, according to advance estimates the Bank of Korea released on Tuesday. The central bank had forecast in August that growth would reach only 0.3 percent in the third quarter. The figures were published on October 27, 2026, by Al Jazeera, which reported them from the bank's data.

Exports, which make up about 45 percent of the country's GDP, rose 2.3 percent from the prior quarter, led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment. Investment in facilities rose 4.1 percent and investment in intellectual property rose 2.3 percent, while construction investment edged up 0.7 percent. Private consumption, however, fell 0.2 percent despite the gains in exports and investment. Taken together, the quarter's results put the economy on course for its fastest expansion in more than a decade.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth of 3.4 to 3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest annual performance since 2011 excluding the COVID-19 pandemic. The economy had grown only 1 percent in 2025, its slowest pace since the pandemic. The article credits the rebound to a global shortage of memory chips, which has benefited South Korea's industry. South Korean exports in September jumped 83.5 percent from a year earlier to $120.9 billion, with chips making up nearly half of all shipments, according to the Korea Customs Service.

South Korea is home to two of the world's three largest memory chip makers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. The two companies together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory. Asia's fourth-largest economy has therefore been well placed to profit from the surge in demand for AI hardware. The article does not describe any further policy steps or forecasts beyond the current estimates.

stories.Headline: NetChoice Urges Colorado AG to Keep ADMT and Chatbot Rules Within the Statutes the Legislature Wrote
stories.Summary:
NetChoice has filed comments with the Colorado Attorney General's Office on revised draft rules that would carry out two state laws, the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act (SB 26-189) and the Chatbot Safety Act (HB 26-1263). The filing was posted on October 26, 2026, and was written by Patrick Hedger, the group's Director of Policy. The comments say the Office made real improvements since its August draft, and several of those changes answer points NetChoice raised in earlier filings. The group's central concern is that the revised rules still go beyond what the legislature wrote into the statutes. According to the comments, the revised rules still add several obligations that the General Assembly considered and chose not to include.

These include new categories of regulated parties, broader disclosure and data-access duties, and prescriptive requirements for how products must be designed. The rules also contain reporting mandates that reach past the subjects the two statutes actually name. NetChoice argues that each of these points should be resolved in favor of the statutory language rather than the expanded draft. NetChoice's position, as paraphrased from the filing, is that the Attorney General's Office should keep its rules tied to the text the legislature adopted. The group asks the Office to make that correction on each of the points it identifies.

The comments are presented as testimony and form part of the public rulemaking record. The filing comes as Colorado moves to put both laws into operation through formal rules, and it adds to a body of NetChoice work on AI rulemaking in the state. The articles do not say when the Attorney General's Office will issue final rules or whether it will adopt NetChoice's proposed changes. The source material also does not describe any response from the Office to the comments.

stories.Headline: RTX Spark: Local AI Coding Fails, I’ve Had (More Than) a Few ⭐
stories.Summary:
Thurrott.com and ZDNET have both published hands-on accounts of Nvidia's RTX Spark laptops, testing whether local AI can handle coding work. Paul Thurrott, writing on October 27, 2026, said he has spent many days trying to find a local AI coding setup on the RTX Spark that works consistently, and that he has only scored occasional small wins. He tested Llama Windows, a graphical front end to the llama.cpp inference engine, which Hugging Face timed to the launch of the RTX Spark computers earlier in the month. Thurrott described the setup as complex and said he had been repeating experiments with different tools and models almost every day for weeks.

David Gewirtz, writing for ZDNET on October 26, 2026, tested Lenovo's Yoga 9n 2-in-1, a 16-inch laptop priced at $4,000 with a 20-core processor, 64GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. He compared it with his own 2025 Mac Studio, which has 128GB of unified memory and cost $5,300. In benchmarks, the Mac delivered about 1.3 times the CPU performance of the Lenovo, and the Lenovo was about three times faster at prompt processing. The Mac pulled ahead on token generation, however, running about 2.5 times faster on a 32-billion-parameter model, which Gewirtz attributed to the Lenovo's smaller memory pool. He ran a local coding agent, OpenCode, with an 80-billion-parameter Qwen coder model and a 32,768-token context window, the largest he could make work with Windows and the model loaded.

Gewirtz reported that the laptop was able to take Mac-only source code for an icon gallery app and, without a spec or screenshots, produce a rough Windows version within about four hours, though he noted much more work would be needed before it could be distributed. He said the constant context refreshes were tedious, and he credited the machine with staying cool during four hours of heavy work. In a battery stress test, the laptop ran a custom CPU and memory workload for one hour and 20 minutes from a full charge before shutting down, and its fan was loud enough to hear from the next room. Thurrott's account offers the more skeptical view, while Gewirtz's report shows that local coding can work on this hardware with real limits on memory and battery life.

stories.Headline: Freedom Holding is developing a $2bn sovereign AI hub in Kazakhstan
stories.Summary:
Freedom Holding Corp., the Nasdaq-listed group, said on Monday, 26 October 2026, that it is advancing plans for a $2 billion Sovereign AI Hub in Kazakhstan and for its first public GPU cloud in 2027. The project is being developed under an agreement signed in November 2025 with Kazakhstan's Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. The announcement followed a meeting on 23 October in Astana between Freedom's chief executive, Timur Turlov, and Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, during Huang's first visit to the country. Turlov presented Freedom's technology businesses and its AI infrastructure plans at the meeting.

The hub is planned with 100MW of available power and is meant to support AI model training, large-scale data processing and AI services for business and government. Freedom's first GPU cluster is due to open to businesses and developers as a public cloud in 2027. A separate Freedom AI Super Cluster, aimed at government, business and science, is scheduled to begin its first phase in the first quarter of 2027. A new Freedom Cloud data centre is under construction near Almaty, and Freedom Cloud already serves more than 3,400 business and public-sector clients. Turlov also said Freedom is placing an order for its first Nvidia B300 computing cluster, according to The Times of Central Asia, although the company's own statement does not name a chip supplier for the hub.

Freedom is the principal financing and implementation partner and will operate the hub. Turlov said demand already stands at twice the planned capacity of the hub's first stage, and the company said major prospective clients are willing to lease future capacity for five years. He added that Kazakhstan has a strong pool of talent already building technology in e-commerce and finance, which, together with domestic AI infrastructure, is becoming one of the country's main advantages. Freedom described its role as providing the infrastructure to help local businesses and developers turn that expertise into AI applications and digital products. The Times of Central Asia noted that the proposal was described as nonbinding in the company's August 2026 filing.

Freedom is part of a wider push in Kazakhstan, where Huang also met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and discussed the country's AI strategy with Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev. Kazakhtelecom has already deployed 400 H200 and 480 B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty, and Firebird signed an investment agreement for a project that Nvidia said has a U.S. export license for 45,000 Grace Blackwell GPUs, with a commercial launch targeted for the third quarter of 2027. Separately, the Turlov-backed Akashi data center campus in Astana is under construction with up to 100 megawatts planned and first-phase operations due in 2027, and the Eurasian Development Bank announced $31.2 million in financing for it on 19 October. Other governments are chasing similar sovereign AI goals, with Nvidia and Palantir having begun selling a sovereign AI stack in September.

Kelvin Bell, founder and CEO of Stratos Digital, won the top prize at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock's second annual artificial intelligence pitch competition, which was sponsored by Amazon Web Services. Bell's project is a bilingual AI agent that helps restaurants answer phone calls, take orders, answer menu questions and suggest additional purchases. Victor AI is built to understand a restaurant's menu well enough to accept phone orders and try one up-sell per order, with the goal of raising the business's profit margins.

Bell said the prize will be crucial to developing the platform, which he said addresses an industry with high operating costs and low profit margins. He also said he has been interested in technology since he was seven years old. Bell already has two restaurants in Arkansas using the service, which lets staff focus on food preparation and other operations while the AI agent handles phone calls. Other winners were Ashley Franke, founder of The Rockin' Chair, who took second place and $35,000 in services, and James Hensley, whose company On Paper took third place and $25,000 in technical development services. Franke's platform gathers accessibility information about live event venues in one place for customers with disabilities, and she hopes to fund it through partnerships with venues so it stays free for fans.

Hensley's app lets people under probation or parole upload an image of their supervision conditions and receives reminders about responsibilities and appointments. Hensley said about 70,000 Arkansans are currently under supervision. The competition comes as UALR expands its AI offerings, including a bachelor's degree in AI launched this fall, which the university describes as the first of its kind at a public university in Arkansas. stories.Headline: AI Can Draw Any Building. But Can It Imagine One?
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by Sixth Tone in August 2026, describes architect Peter Guohua Fu's experiment with artificial intelligence. He had been prompted by a friend, Canadian composer Steve Barakatt, whose AI-generated design of a "piano café" surprised him. Fu then used AI to produce a two-hour film, "The Architect with Three Shades of Blue," recounting his career and the completion of "Music on the River" in Hengqin. The team was ten people, and the film cost under 200,000 yuan, or $29,650, and took less than two months to finish.

Fu's conclusion is that AI excels at execution but cannot originate ideas. He notes that the later stages of architectural design, such as detailed development and technical drawings, are where AI is most useful, and he cites a 2025 Royal Institute of British Architects report showing AI adoption among practices rose from 41% in 2024 to 59% in 2025. He estimates that large firms in China and Canada may already exceed 80%. Yet he argues that concept design remains beyond AI, since the tool can only recombine what already exists. He expects the profession to split toward two extremes: rare, original thinkers at one end and a growing number of people who can visualize their ideas at the other.

Fu also voices concern about education and development. He says that students at Tongji University and McGill's School of Architecture, where he has taught, have suddenly submitted work of remarkable quality, and he does not know whether they used AI but worries that they may not be building independent thinking skills. He describes this as a paradox, since excellent architects may need only a strong idea and the ability to direct AI, yet fewer people may gain the experience that produces such ideas. He also observes that the barrier to entry is falling, because anyone with aesthetic judgment can now generate a building image. Most such images will never be built, he concedes, and he recalls an abandoned underwater theater design that he later had his son recreate in a video game.

The second article, dated October 27, 2026 and reported by Jang Ji-seung for Seoul Economic Daily, covers a different AI development. Researchers led by Professor Baek Seung-ryeol at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, working with the University of Aberdeen, created "FlexiAvatar," a system that builds 3D avatars from footage showing only part of a body. Existing methods assumed the whole body was visible, so upper-body or face-only video produced distorted results. The team combined a body model called SMPL-X with a rendering method known as 3D Gaussian splatting, and it used generative AI to supply unseen views such as the back of the head while weighting real footage more heavily. The work was presented at the European Conference on Computer Vision in Malmo, Sweden, in September 2026, and it was supported by South Korean government bodies including the National Research Foundation of Korea.

According to the report, FlexiAvatar outperformed comparison technologies on image quality measured in PSNR across all filming ranges. On the NeuMan full-body dataset it scored 35.77 dB against 34.80 dB for ExAvatar, and on real-world full-body footage it scored 30.98 dB against 28.65 dB for ToMiE. For face-focused footage the number of 3D components fell from 167,390 to 84,095, data size dropped 49.8% to 4.49 MB, and rendering speed rose about 34% to 39.15 frames per second. The report notes that total production time and graphics memory use did not fall by the same proportion, and the team plans further work on rendering loose clothing. Baek said the technology could serve video conferencing, virtual reality, films and games.

stories.Headline: Wang Yi Calls for China-U.S. Cooperation to Develop and Govern AI
stories.Summary:
On Friday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said China and the United States both have the capacity and the responsibility to develop and govern artificial intelligence together. He made the remarks in Xiong'an New Area in Hebei province during a meeting with John L. Thornton, co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society, and Thomas L. Friedman, a New York Times columnist. The two visitors were in China for the 2026 Global Governance Forum. According to China's Foreign Ministry, the meeting took place in late October 2026.

Wang argued that the two leading AI countries should cooperate not only to guard against risks but also to agree on rules and standards that could be applied worldwide. He said such rules should keep the technology under human control and allow it to serve people, promoting shared prosperity and common security. He added that China favors inclusive AI development that serves the common good. The aim, in his account, is to ensure the technology benefits people across the world rather than a narrow group of states.

Wang also placed AI within a wider discussion of global governance, saying the world faces several deficits, including in peace, development and security. He described the Global Governance Initiative as an important public good that has won broad international recognition and support. He praised Thornton and Friedman for their long-standing efforts to promote relations between China and the United States, and he expressed hope that they would help make the forum a success. Their involvement, he suggested, reflects the kind of engagement he wants to encourage.

A Foreign Ministry press release quoted Thornton and Friedman as saying that the malicious use of AI poses the greatest risk to building a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the two countries. They hoped Beijing and Washington would deepen cooperation on the issue and offer an important public good to the world. The two also said the international community is closely following the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting that China will host. They expressed the hope that China would use that occasion to play a distinctive and positive role in addressing global challenges.

stories.Headline: SK hynix Unveils 3D FeNAND for AI Computing
stories.Summary:
SK hynix has developed a memory technology that carries out artificial intelligence calculations inside NAND flash memory itself. The company disclosed the research on analog computing-in-memory using ferroelectric three-dimensional NAND, known as 3D FeNAND, in a newsroom post on October 14. The findings were published in a paper by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. The approach performs multiply-accumulate operations, the basic building blocks of AI computing, within the memory, which reduces how much data must move around.

Ferroelectric materials keep their internal polarization after an external electric field is removed, and FeNAND uses these polarization states to store data and control current. Conventional 3D NAND relies on a charge-trap nitride structure that holds electrons in a nitride layer. According to SK hynix, FeNAND can produce several current states within one cell, which makes it well suited to representing the weights used in AI computations. The researchers tuned cells, the surrounding non-cell circuits and pages together to improve this computing performance.

In simulations, the 3D FeNAND-based design reached up to 20 times the throughput and 5,000 times the energy efficiency of conventional nonvolatile memory. At the cell level, the team sets different current states by changing the number of programming pulses at a constant voltage, whereas conventional NAND raises the voltage. At the circuit level, the researchers reduced wordline resistance by introducing air gaps between wordlines, which select and control memory cells. At the page level, they optimized data placement and computation order, using in-page pipelining to run neural network computations efficiently within a single page.

The same period brought broader market context. Seoul Economic Daily reported on October 27 that SK hynix planned to announce a large shareholder return package with its third-quarter earnings on the 28th, including its first special dividend, with more than 50 percent of free cash flow under consideration. The report also noted that the company's stock had fallen to 1.275 million won, less than half its June peak. Whether the chip technology translates into commercial products, and how the market values that work, remains to be seen in the coming quarters.

Google Cloud and Oracle used Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on October 27, 2026 to announce an expanded partnership that links Oracle's database and application products with Google's data and AI services. The announcement centers on connecting Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud with Google's Agentic Data Cloud and Gemini Enterprise. Google Cloud's product manager for databases, Kunal Agarwal, wrote the post describing these changes.

Several capabilities were announced as building blocks for this work. A remote Model Context Protocol server for Oracle workloads, built on an IAM-governed ExecuteSQL Data API, is now generally available and resolves database credentials through Secret Manager. A Knowledge Catalog integration is in preview and is meant to unify metadata discovery and governance across Oracle databases and the wider Google platform. The companies described these tools as a way to let AI agents act on live operational data without custom middleware, plaintext passwords or manual data copies. They also said Gemini models are being embedded in Oracle Fusion AI Agent Studio, Fusion Claw, Oracle Fusion Applications and NetSuite. Google Cloud and Oracle named Argano, Automus, Calfus, HCL, IBM, Infosys, LTM, Pythian, TCS and Tessell as partners that will supply pre-built skills, connectors and industry blueprints. On the data side, a bi-directional Apache Iceberg integration in preview lets Oracle and Google's borderless Lakehouse query and write shared tables in Google Cloud Storage, and native OCI GoldenGate integration streams change data into BigQuery with sub-second freshness. A BigQuery query federation feature with Oracle, also in preview, allows live Oracle queries from BigQuery without copying data.

The post also reported new regions and compliance plans.
