stories.Headline: Reddit's Largest Open-Source Community Imposes Full AI Ban: Linux and Python Content Delisted Immediately
stories.Summary:
Reddit's largest open-source community, r/opensource, announced a sweeping ban on AI-related content on October 24, 2026, through a pinned post by moderator u/Wolvereness. The rules bar any project that uses AI, is written by AI, or is designed to serve AI, and they also name and ban MCP, which affects open-source agent tools. Under the new rules, a project must have been actively maintained for at least one year and have more than three contributors, and the poster's Reddit account must be at least a year old with substantial history. The moderator also barred non-native English speakers from posting, saying the community cannot tell AI-written content from AI-translated content.

The rules also create a dead loop for new projects, since a developer needs three contributors to qualify but cannot post a request to recruit them. Posts seeking maintainers or contributors are no longer accepted at all. Anyone who messages the moderator to plead for an exception faces an immediate permanent ban, and only officially registered non-profit entities such as 501(c) organizations may apply for exemption in advance. The post also carried a harsh tone, telling people that token use did not matter and that they should leave if they disliked the policy. Critics noted that the restrictions would exclude many long-running projects that use no AI at all.

The strongest objection came from the tech community, which pointed out that Linux would fall under the ban. Commenters on the post and on Kotaku's coverage argued that the rule would exclude the Linux kernel, which Linus Torvalds has been developing with Claude Code. On October 10, Torvalds submitted eight kernel patches created in a branch with the assistance of that tool, and he publicly said AI can make programming more fun when used correctly. The moderator later blamed the backlash on an opinion piece from The Lunduke Journal that pointed hundreds of readers to the thread. The Linux kernel documentation, by contrast, requires human review and a Signed-off-by label on every merged change.

The controversy shows a split in how open-source communities define acceptable tools, and the community's rules remain in force as the debate continues. Tech blogger chasm listed 38 major open-source projects, from Linux and Python to Git, Docker and Firefox, that the rules would place out of reach of discussion. Kotaku reported that many commenters said the policy was orthogonal to open source itself, since disliking AI does not change whether a project is open source. The reporting does not say whether the moderators will revise the rules, so their future remains unclear.

stories.Headline: Colorado AG Urged to Delay AI Hiring Disclosures, Tighten Terms
stories.Summary:
Business groups in Colorado have asked the state attorney general to hold off on enforcing the state's law governing artificial intelligence decision-making tools until rulemaking is finished. They also want the definitions of "data sources," a tool's "material influence" on decisions, and "meaningful human review" revised. The request was reported on October 26, 2026, based on coverage of the attorney general's proposal. The groups are pressing these changes while the office works on the rules.

The attorney general's office is finalizing requirements that would apply when businesses use AI tools to reject someone's job, credit, or housing application. Under the rules, those businesses would have to provide detailed disclosures and give applicants appeal rights. The proposal is a transparency-focused rewrite of a sweeping algorithmic bias law that never took effect. The office held a public hearing on its latest draft on the Monday before the reporting date, where testimony was taken on the revised text. The articles do not give the number of comments received or the deadlines for final rules.

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser leads the office responsible for the rulemaking, and the business groups are the ones urging the delay and changes. The articles do not record any direct statement from Weiser or the groups beyond the substance of their requests. The reporting frames the disagreement as one over how precisely the law's key terms should be defined before the rules take effect. Coverage of the broader debate over the law itself, including the reasons it never took effect, is not included in these articles.

The articles do not say whether the attorney general will accept the requested delay or the proposed definitional changes. They also do not indicate when a final rule will be issued or when any enforcement would begin. What happens next will depend on how the office responds to the testimony it received and the revisions it makes to its draft. Any changes to the draft would determine how businesses using AI hiring and lending tools must comply.

stories.Headline: Estonia criticizes bill on registering AI agents
stories.Summary:
Estonia has prepared amendments that would let people register special "agent codes" for AI agents, and the proposal has drawn criticism from technology companies, lawyers and government agencies. The report, published on October 26, 2026 by ua.news and citing ERR News, describes critics who consider the document insufficiently developed and point to potential threats to digital security. An AI agent, unlike a chatbot, receives a task and independently seeks a way to complete it. Such tools could help with tax returns, analysing bank accounts, mobile tariffs or searching for airline tickets. Giving agents access to bank card data, the report notes, may create security risks.

Minister of Economy and Industry Liina Vahtras said the state does not plan to give AI agents a separate digital identity. Instead, a person would register an additional agent code so that information systems can tell apart their own actions from operations a program carries out on their behalf. These codes would be entered into a centralized database to verify which agent acts for which person. An earlier idea of letting companies register agents, and letting one person hold several, was dropped. At the first stage, an individual could register only one agent.

The legislative amendments are planned to go to the Riigikogu in early November. Cybernetica, a company that helped build Estonia's e-government infrastructure, submitted 11 pages of comments and said the bill contains contradictions, will not reach its stated goals in its current form and may be dangerous. Its development manager, Arne Ansper, argued that simple registration is not enough, and that agents need authentication and signing mechanisms with protection comparable to ID cards, Mobile-ID or Smart-ID. He warned that giving agents broad powers at a lower level of protection would weaken overall digital security. The Estonian Association of Information Technology and Telecommunications also urged that the document not advance in its current form.

Its president, Ats Albre, raised uncertainty over liability when an agent submits user data to state authorities, and he believes ultimate responsibility should stay with the person. According to ERR News, no ministry had approved the bill by the deadline, and only the State Chancellery had signed off. Vahtras said legal, communications and technical working groups are working in parallel and that the initiative itself may still be revised. The story suggests the debate is still open, with the timing of the November submission depending on how the criticism is addressed.

Articles.Title: Estonia criticizes bill on registering AI agents

stories.Headline: Legal Tech Co. Clio Says AI Co. Can't Revive Lapsed Data Deal
stories.Summary:
Legal tech company Clio has asked a federal court in Virginia to rule that it is not obligated to renew a case law data arrangement it once had with Ross, an artificial intelligence research platform. The request was reported by Law360 on October 26, 2026, and it concerns a data feed that Clio previously shared with Ross, which has since lapsed. The articles describe the dispute as Clio seeking a declaration that the expired deal cannot be revived by the AI company. The filing sets out Clio's position that the lapse ended its duty to continue supplying the material. The reporting available here does not give further details about the terms of the original agreement or the specific dates it expired.

Clio's request asks the court to settle a question about whether a lapsed data agreement can be brought back into force at the demand of the other party. In asking for that declaration, Clio is seeking a legal finding that it has no continuing obligation to re-up the case law feed. The articles do not list any dollar amounts, contract durations, or other figures tied to the arrangement. They also do not indicate whether Ross has responded to the filing or what remedy it has sought. Because the court has not yet ruled, the practical effect of any outcome is not described in the available coverage.

The party bringing the action is Clio, which is the legal tech company that filed the request in the Virginia federal court. Ross, the AI research platform on the other side of the arrangement, is the party whose effort to revive the data deal is at the center of the dispute. The Law360 article by Matt Perez reports the filing but the portions visible to us do not include statements from either company beyond the core position that the deal cannot be revived. Neither the articles nor the page material provided includes direct comments attributed to executives at Clio or Ross. Accordingly, the account of each company's stance rests on the filing as summarized in the coverage.

The matter sits within a broader pattern of legal technology firms and AI developers negotiating over access to legal content such as case law, which is why a lapsed data arrangement has drawn attention. The Law360 piece is filed under its Daily Litigation and Legal Tech and AI sections, signaling its relevance to both courtroom disputes and the business of legal technology. The articles do not describe any prior rulings in the case or how the court is expected to proceed. stories.Headline: How agentic AI could streamline KYC processes by up to 70% in banking efficiency - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Agentic artificial intelligence could cut the time banks spend on know-your-customer checks by 30 to 70 per cent, according to a McKinsey & Company report published on October 27, 2026 and reported by ETCIO. The report says the technology could improve efficiency in financial-crime prevention, but it also notes that high costs for human oversight, along with governance and accuracy concerns, continue to slow wider adoption. It points out that banks often assign 10 to 15 per cent of their employees to know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering work alone. Institutions are now turning to agentic AI to address that burden. The coverage was carried by ANI and the piece was posted on the ETCIO site.

The report describes several problems that must be managed before the gains can be realised. Financial institutions often lack adequate metrics to judge AI reasoning and agent behaviour, even though such evaluations are relatively inexpensive because they do not require labelled data. One bank ran ten evaluations across its customer onboarding process, setting minimum thresholds of 80 per cent accuracy and 70 per cent consistency. Measured consistency across published evaluations ranged from 72 to 100 per cent, and on the weakest system roughly one run in four gave a different answer to the same input. The report also finds that human supervision accounts for 70 to 75 per cent of variable-run costs in a customer service task, while token costs make up only 20 to 25 per cent.

McKinsey suggests that these costs could be reduced by more than half through measures such as using cheaper AI models for simpler tasks, removing duplicate operations, cutting data transfers between agents, and moving from checking every output to sample-based quality reviews. It cautions, however, that lowering the frequency of quality checks in regulated banking functions requires careful judgment because such decisions involve compliance and risk management, not only technology. The report argues that a human in the loop is no longer enough to ensure reliable oversight as banks expand their use of autonomous systems, and it attributes this to supervisory requirements. Its overall conclusion is that agentic AI has moved from concept to production in financial-crime prevention faster than most institutions expected, and that the value is real, although the industry is still at an early stage.

stories.Headline: UBS says it does not permit the use of external AI models for client transactions - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
UBS has said it will not allow external AI models to carry out transactions on behalf of its clients. The statement came from CEO Sergio Ermotti on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, as reported by Reuters and carried by ET CIO. Ermotti spoke at a science conference, where he addressed the bank's stance on the use of such systems. The announcement follows wider concern in the banking sector that advanced AI agents could harm the financial system.

Ermotti pointed to recent reports that some banks have been exposed to possible misbehavior by AI models that manage client accounts, shift deposits, and optimize deposits. He said UBS is not allowing models to enter the bank and perform those tasks. He also stressed that the most important issue in AI right now is ensuring that models do not drive outcomes for clients inside a black box. The articles report that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, according to people familiar with the matter.

Ermotti framed the policy as a matter of caution about opaque systems rather than a rejection of technology. He said UBS remains committed to advancing its technology after its integration of Credit Suisse, which it acquired in 2023. That integration had forced the bank to slow its AI deployment somewhat. Ermotti said he was glad the integration is nearly complete, which will let the bank place more emphasis on technology to become more effective and efficient.

stories.Headline: Bridging Relationship Gaps: "Companion Star" AI Dating Practice Partner & Real-Person Soul Matching Service – Empower 240 Million Singles to Master Proper Dating Chat Before Meaningful Matches
stories.Summary:
Shaanxi Hongtu Youcheng Network Technology Co., Ltd. has launched BanXing, a friendship-oriented communication skill community that combines AI dating practice partners with real-person soul matching, and it is currently seeking angel round financing. The product was introduced in October 2026 and is aimed at single people who struggle to keep conversations going. Its founder, Li Ning, built the idea around the view that many singles lack the ability to chat and maintain a relationship rather than a way to meet people. The company has framed the service as a place to learn conversation first and get matched afterward.

The platform lets users first practice chatting with multiple AI dating partners that have distinct personalities, careers, interests and memories, and a system reminds users when they stop contacting someone for a long time. Users then move into anonymous real-person matching based on chat profiles rather than appearance, with users in the same city given priority. The system reviews chat records on a daily rolling basis and produces a communication ability report that cites specific dialogue and offers targeted suggestions. The product has been fully developed and deployed online, with 208 back-end interface tests passed and 20 AI dating partners connected, and it is built on a self-developed back end that connects to the Moonshot Kimi large model. The company is not charging for the service for now and is focused on user growth before adding paid features.

Li Ning is responsible for product development and financing, and he has long experience in store informatization and local merchant services in Shaanxi. In explaining his reasons for starting the business, he said many single people are not unwilling to fall in love but are afraid of saying the wrong thing or harming a relationship, and he sees helping them take the first step as the project's main purpose. The company is recruiting partners in technology, operations and product design. The round being sought is 1 million to 3 million yuan, covering 18 months, with about 60% for product and AI computing costs, about 25% for user acquisition and operations, and about 15% for compliance, legal and reserves.

The product comes as China's single population is estimated at 240 million and marriage registrations have fallen sharply from their 2013 peak, and as AI companion apps such as Xingye and Maoxiang have shown strong user engagement. The company's plan sets a first-year target of 1 million registered users among singles aged 18 to 35 in first- and second-tier cities, with seed user verification in the first four months and a 25% seven-day retention goal. The articles also note that the Interim Measures for the Administration of Artificial Intelligence Anthropomorphic Interactive Services took effect in July 2026, and that two miHoYo AI companion products were suspended in August 2026. Whether BanXing secures the financing and meets its milestones has not been reported.

stories.Headline: Hundreds of Billions in AI Capital Pours In Yet Investment Yields Zero Returns
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek has raised another 100 billion yuan, a domestic record for a single AI financing round, with Tencent and CATL leading it. The round was reportedly oversubscribed, lifting the target from 500 billion yuan to nearly 1 trillion yuan at a pre-money valuation of about 5 trillion yuan. Around the same time, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok said that outside the tech giants, AI has produced no financial returns for U.S. companies. Figures for 493 non-tech firms in the S&P 500 showed flat per capita revenue, flat profit margins and no lift in productivity.

The funds are meant to build computing power infrastructure rather than just fund a model. DeepSeek plans a data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, deploying at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend chips for frontier model pre-training on domestic hardware. Tencent, which has invested in two consecutive rounds, is seeking an early position as its messaging, gaming and cloud businesses connect to model capabilities. CATL's stake is tied to electricity, the largest cost of computing power, through data center power supply, energy storage and green power. Other backers named in the reporting include SMIC PES, Stony Creek Capital and Geely.

Apollo's data also showed that AI spending is concentrated. The top 10% of enterprises account for 99.5% of spending on model services and inference, and among the top 1% of spenders, 80.4% have venture capital backing. Slok argued that mainstream firms are beginning to treat token spending as a cost center that erodes profit rather than a growth source. The reporting also cites S&P Global Market Intelligence, which estimated that about 42% of corporate AI projects were eventually abandoned. OpenAI shut down its Sora video platform and folded other products into its main application, while numerous startups have closed or been acquired.

The article draws a parallel with autonomous driving, where more than 40 companies exited between 2019 and 2026 after financing dried up and commercialization never arrived. It warns that humanoid robotics and embodied intelligence, which DeepSeek has also invested in, are following a similar path. The author argues that Tencent and CATL are less betting on AI applications than on infrastructure, and that the real test will come when the S&P 493 profit figures show AI creating value for the broader economy. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tesla to Build 20,000-Robot AI Training Cluster with Total Investment of Around 14 Billion Yuan
stories.Summary:
Tesla has postponed mass production of its Optimus humanoid robot to around the end of 2027, according to comments made during its Q3 2026 earnings call, which Chezhi reviewed and reported on October 26, 2026. Under the revised plan, external deliveries will not begin before then, and all Optimus units built earlier will be used only inside Tesla. Before mass production, the company will make roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots for an Optimus Academy, a training cluster it is building to collect data and let the robots learn autonomously. The report estimates the project's total cost at around 14 billion yuan.

The article says the delay stems mainly from the dexterous hand, which currently wears out and must be scrapped after about one month of use, falling short of commercial durability. Tesla is still custom-developing some components to fix reliability, and the company expects these problems to be solved by the end of 2027. The "brain" side is further along, with the AI5 chip expected to be mounted on Optimus around April 2027, and the chip is described as roughly ten times more powerful than the AI4. The reasoning behind the training cluster is that, unlike FSD, which learns from data gathered across millions of sold vehicles, Optimus must first build robots to generate its own training data. The author estimates each unit could cost 50,000 to 100,000 US dollars, well above the roughly 30,000 dollar target.

Elon Musk has said Optimus and Robotaxi are the two pillars of Tesla's valuation, and he has asked people to temper their expectations because the robot is not yet finalized. He compared the robot hand unfavorably with the human hand, which is soft, sensor-rich and able to repair itself, and said Tesla intends to have Optimus learn through large-scale practice, much as a child does. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of AI software, said that because no comparable training setup exists, Optimus must first observe how tasks are done before practicing them itself. Musk also said a video of Optimus performing without pre-programmed routines would be released within one to two months. The article notes that, given Tesla's track record, the schedule could slip further, and that by the end of 2027 customers outside Tesla will most likely use the robots for dangerous, repetitive or round-the-clock industrial work before home use expands.

stories.Headline: When AI Outperforms Humans in Verbal Communication, Agora Builds the Invisible Path for Intelligent Interaction
stories.Summary:
Agora used its RTE2026 conference, which has been upgraded to iRTE, to put forward a new framework for real-time AI voice interaction on October 26, 2026. The announcement centers on the company's real-time AI infrastructure, which it says addresses the practical difficulty of making voice agents interact naturally. The articles describe a familiar frustration: voice assistants pause before answering, ignore mid-sentence corrections and keep a flat tone even when a user is impatient. The company frames this lag as a real-time problem rather than an intelligence problem.

The articles set out how fast the market has moved in roughly two and a half years. OpenAI introduced GPT-4o real-time voice in May 2024, released its Realtime API that October, and moved it into production last August. In 2026, further models added real-time reasoning, tool calling and parallel dialogue and task execution. Sierra, an enterprise voice agent company, raised $950 million in May at a valuation of $15.8 billion and reported ARR above $150 million, with billing shifting to a per-problem-solved model. Grand View Research estimates the global AI voice agent market at about $2.54 billion in 2025, rising to $35.2 billion by 2033, with a 39% compound annual growth rate from 2026 to 2033.

Agora's own account ties the conference to its history. The event began in 2015 as the Real-time Internet Conference, was renamed RTE in 2020, and is now iRTE, with the "i" standing for real-time intelligence. The organizers say this reflects two extensions: interaction now includes people talking to AI agents, and content now includes carrying intelligence as well as transmitting information. The program lists more than 15 forums and over 100 talks, with speakers from model makers including Kimi, MiniMax and StepFun, and from companies such as Meituan, Alibaba ATH, Rokid and Soul. Agora's chief executive, Zhao Bin, is quoted as saying conversational AI is pushing real-time communication from normal dialogue toward vivid, expressive interaction.

Zhao Bin also proposed a five-level framework for conversational capability, moving from passive expression based on the speaker's own perspective, through active coherence, personalized adaptation, complex multi-person communication, up to tacit understanding based on deep relationships. Agora says its product line has built on this since its AIGC RTC SDK in October 2023, including support for OpenAI's Realtime API in October 2024. The company describes its Agora Conversational Model as a hybrid of a perception system, a full-duplex dialogue response system and an expression model. Its customers are named as including MiniMax, SenseTime, Zhipu AI and Meituan. The articles present these as company claims and do not independently verify the performance figures.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Seeks $100 Billion in First AI Model Maker IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI model developer, filed a registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, seeking a Nasdaq listing, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal cited by Seoul Economic Daily. The company is reportedly targeting an initial public offering that would raise $100 billion at a valuation of up to $2 trillion. That figure would exceed the $1.77 trillion valuation and $86 billion raised when SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq on June 12 of this year. If the listing goes ahead, Anthropic would be the first AI model company to enter the U.S. stock market, and Wall Street sees a strong chance that trading could begin in mid-November, between the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 and Thanksgiving on November 26.

The filing presents both the promise and the risks of AI, citing productivity gains it estimates could reach $22.5 trillion by 2031 and support for treating rare diseases. It also lists risks including AI-driven doomsday scenarios, friction with the Trump administration, bottlenecks in the semiconductor supply chain and slowing earnings growth. Anthropic says its contracts with chip and data center companies total more than $800 billion, with investment periods running to 2045. Its largest computing contract is with Broadcom, a five-year, $161.2 billion deal to co-develop Google's tensor processing unit and lease it to Anthropic. Google, Amazon and Microsoft are also set to provide at least $269.4 billion in cloud computing over 10 years, costs that must be paid regardless of usage.

Anthropic's leadership, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has pointed to its financial progress in response to profitability concerns. According to the filing, revenue for the first half of the year reached $16.286 billion, more than 14 times the $1.16 billion of the same period last year. Operating losses narrowed 68% to $693 million, and adjusted operating profit of $1.618 billion marked the company's first half-year operating profit since its founding. The company also said its latest model, Claude Opus 5.5, cut token costs per task by about 40%, and that revenue per employee reached $6.6 million, approaching Nvidia's $7 million.

The IPO is expected to be offered in the U.S., Japan, the U.K., Switzerland, Australia, Canada and several European Economic Area countries, with Japanese securities firms under Mizuho and MUFG joining as underwriters. Anthropic said it has not completed the registration required for a public offering in South Korea, so share sales there are limited to private placements and other methods permitted by law. Reuters described the listing as arriving at a critical moment for judging whether AI will generate enough revenue to justify its enormous spending. The filing's details, including the valuation target and timing, remain reports and expectations rather than confirmed terms.

stories.Headline: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers posted a paper on arXiv, a preprint server, describing LocalAgent, a framework for checking whether two images show the exact same physical object. The paper, dated October 27, 2026, was written by Jiachen Guo and six co-authors, including Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin and Ajian Liu. The authors say existing multimodal large language models still struggle with this task when viewpoint, lighting or background changes. They note that semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions, which makes careful local checking necessary.

LocalAgent pairs a general-purpose multimodal model with lightweight specialist verifiers. The general model first reasons over the whole image to flag suspicious local regions, then hands those regions to a Local Evidence Verifier toolkit. That toolkit contains two components: Local Appearance Consistency, which estimates similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence, which estimates spatial matching under viewpoint changes. The toolkit returns structured scalar evidence, which the general model combines into a final decision. The authors also describe an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy that weights answer correctness above tool-use and format signals, so the system learns when verification is needed.

According to the paper, LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest chain-of-thought reinforcement fine-tuning baseline. It invokes a verifier on only 12.13% of samples, and the authors report that it preserves the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying model. The paper says the open-source repository is available online. The work is presented as a preprint and has not, based on the material provided, been peer reviewed or formally published.

Articles.Title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency

stories.Headline: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv, titled "When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts," reports a finding about weight-only post-training quantization, a method for shrinking large language models to low numerical precision. The authors, nine researchers led by Yanlong Zhao, write that the standard practice of minimizing reconstruction loss does not reliably produce better model performance on new tasks. They report that lower reconstruction loss can even degrade performance on the same calibration data used to set the weights. The paper was listed with a date of October 27, 2026, and is categorized under artificial intelligence, machine learning and statistical machine learning.

To address this, the authors propose Distributionally Robust Quantization, abbreviated DRQ, which they describe as a post-hoc refinement step. DRQ adjusts the integer codes that represent quantized weights while staying inside the existing quantization grid, and it leaves the quantization parameters and inference operators unchanged. The method works by minimizing the worst-case reconstruction loss across a constrained set of input activation distributions. According to the abstract, the approach requires no added inference overhead, so a model keeps its running cost after refinement.

The authors state that they carried out extensive experiments in which DRQ improved models quantized by six representative methods, including AWQ, GPTQ and ParoQuant. They say the gains appeared in both dense and mixture-of-experts large language models. The paper presents these results as establishing DRQ as a general refinement framework for weight-only quantization that yields better downstream performance. The abstract does not name the institutional affiliations of the authors or report specific benchmark figures, and the article provides no information on adoption or follow-up work beyond the paper itself.

Articles.Title: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization

stories.Headline: The markets are starting to act seriously weird. Blame AI
stories.Summary:
Stocks in the United States have been behaving in unusual ways, and David Goldman, writing in a CNN Business analysis published October 26, 2026, links the strange moves largely to worries about artificial intelligence. On the surface the market looks steady, with stocks near record highs and bonds roughly where they have been for a couple of months, but Goldman says investors are growing nervous beneath that calm. The key signal came on October 22, when the equal-weighted S&P 500 gained 0.5% while the market-value-weighted index fell 1.2%, a divergence that had occurred only twice before since 1995, on April 14, 1999, and March 30, 2000, according to James Reilly of Capital Economics. The same day, the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5% in its largest single-day drop since March 10, 2023.

Goldman explains that bond yields had been surging for three main reasons: the Iran war and resulting inflation, America's debt, which he puts at $40 trillion with a budget deficit of $2 trillion over the past fiscal year, and heavy AI spending, which runs around $1 trillion a year and is increasingly financed by borrowing. Those pressures have not eased, and the article notes oil prices are at four-year highs and that President Donald Trump has signaled the Iran war may escalate again after the midterms. Even so, investors turned to Treasuries as a safe haven after doubts arose about the AI portion of that picture. The article points to CoreWeave, a debt-funded company renting computing power to AI firms, whose borrowing costs rose to about 15% earlier in October. It also cites a Wall Street Journal report that Anthropic's draft IPO filing showed a loss of nearly $81 billion in the first half of 2026, and says Meta spent $2 billion more cash than it generated in the third quarter, sending its stock down 7% on Thursday.

Goldman writes that these concerns have prompted some traders to question how much value Wall Street places on AI and whether current debt levels are sustainable. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US, is quoted saying the market shows elevated volatility around something that looks like a bubble. The article notes the Nasdaq has slid about 6% over two weeks, but that similar scares in past earnings seasons were followed by renewed buying of AI stocks. It adds that even if an AI bubble bursts, the broader economy might not follow, because recent sectoral booms and busts have balanced one another in what some economists call a rolling recession. Goldman concludes that it is unclear whether this episode marks the start of something larger or is just another bump in the road.

Articles.Title: The markets are starting to act seriously weird. Blame AI

stories.Headline: IBM Integration Intelligence Hub gives AI the context to act, not just access
stories.Summary:
IBM has published an article describing its new Integration Intelligence Hub, which is designed to give AI coding assistants and agents the enterprise context they need before they act on integration assets. The piece, dated 26 October 2026, argues that letting an AI agent reach a tool is not enough, because the agent also needs to know what integrations already exist, which ones are current and endorsed, what depends on them, who owns them, and what the agent is permitted to change. IBM frames this as the gap between access and understanding, and says the Hub is meant to close it. The Hub combines three capabilities that the article names as Asset Explorer, Skills and IBM DataPower Interact Gateway. Asset Explorer gives the agent context about integration assets, including what they mean, how they connect, who owns them and which are trusted.

Skills act as runbooks written for AI, giving assistants a repeatable way to follow practices that are often held in documentation or by experienced specialists. Interact Gateway serves as the policy enforcement point for identity, access, audit and approved actions, and higher-risk actions can stay subject to human oversight. The article also describes progressive disclosure, in which an assistant starts with a few entry tools and receives only the skills and tools relevant to the task at hand. The article is written by IBM's own product staff, Jiri De Jagere, a Product Manager for Strategy and AI, and Jigdesh Sampath, a Product Marketing Manager, and it presents the Hub as part of a broader set of AI capabilities across IBM Integration. It names FlowPilot, which brings MCP tools and agent skills into development environments, and says the Hub builds on these as well as on Interact Gateway's governed traffic handling.

IBM also states that it plans to introduce the Hub initially as a SaaS capability within IBM Integration, with wider product and deployment coverage to follow over time. The article offers a worked example, a purchase-order integration using SAP and Kafka, to show how the assistant with enterprise context identifies a dependent B2B process and pauses before deleting a flow. The piece places the Hub within a wider shift the article describes, in which gateways, integration platforms and agentic orchestration are converging as enterprises seek more consistent ways for AI to interact with their systems. It does not report any independent evaluation, customer results or pricing, so the claims about the Hub's benefits rest on IBM's own description. IBM says it will expand the Hub's product and deployment coverage over time, but the article gives no timetable for that expansion.

Articles.Title: IBM Integration Intelligence Hub gives AI the context to act, not just access

stories.Headline: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration
stories.Summary:
Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, according to official data released on Tuesday. Firms with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($2.8 million) reported combined profits of 6.03 trillion yuan from January to September. The National Bureau of Statistics said profits grew 14.4 percent in September alone. Industrial production stayed steady, and cumulative profit growth has remained in double digits this year. The electronics industry was the main driver, with its profits doubling year on year over the period and adding 9.6 percentage points to the overall gain.

Demand for artificial intelligence computing power and advanced memory technologies helped push up earnings, with electronic specialty material manufacturing up 220 percent and semiconductor device manufacturing up 51.7 percent. Optoelectronic component and electronic circuit manufacturing rose 69.8 percent and 62.5 percent. High-tech manufacturing profits jumped 52 percent, accounting for 25.5 percent of total industrial profits, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. Optical fiber and optical cable manufacturing profits surged 570 percent and 110 percent, respectively, as computing infrastructure and data center construction expanded.

Raw materials manufacturing also contributed, with profits climbing 44.9 percent and adding 5.9 percentage points to overall growth. Strong demand for copper, aluminum and other metals from AI and new-energy industries lifted nonferrous metals profits by 79.7 percent. Mining profits rose 38.2 percent and manufacturing profits increased 17 percent across the broader sector. Chen Xi, a researcher at the Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission, said large-scale equipment upgrades, the integration of AI into manufacturing and tax policy support have helped firms cut costs and improve efficiency.

He also credited China's comprehensive industrial supply chains and quick response to market demand. The National Bureau of Statistics said it will focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and accelerating the shift from traditional to new growth drivers. The agency framed these goals as ways to strengthen the economy's internal momentum and advance high-quality industrial development. The articles do not specify further policy measures or timelines beyond these stated aims.

Articles.Title: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration - Global Times

stories.Headline: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has unveiled a factory-integrated data center model called DSX POD, announced October 21 at GTC Berlin and built around its Vera Rubin platform. The reference design packages computing, networking, rack-level power and liquid cooling into standardized modular containers that partner manufacturers would integrate, cable and test before shipment. NVIDIA says this could cut deployment time at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries beginning in early 2027. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said an AI factory creates value once it starts producing tokens rather than when construction ends. The move responds to pressure on operators to bring power-dense AI infrastructure online while facing labor shortages and long build schedules.

The announcement is part of a wider push by infrastructure partners toward repeatable, factory-made AI capacity. Armada and Johnson Controls plan a distributed sovereign AI program targeting 500 MW in 2027, with modules built at Armada's Galleon Forge facilities in Gilbert, Arizona, and Dublin, Ireland. Armada CEO Dan Wright said the race in system integration will not be won by whoever pours concrete fastest. Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters also released a time study finding that prefabricated IT pods cut measured onsite installation time from 75.5 hours to about 15 hours per pod, an 80 percent reduction. The companies stress that this figure covers one installation portion, not total construction time.

Responsibility for the design and its rollout sits with NVIDIA, which has built a large partner ecosystem including Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Foxconn, Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Eaton, Crusoe and others. The partners are preparing manufacturing capacity, and Crusoe has opened a modular manufacturing facility in Colorado. Vertiv has also worked on a 41 MW deployment in Norway. The DSX POD design extends NVIDIA's earlier DSX AI Factory architecture, introduced in March, into physical manufacturing rather than replacing site and facility systems. The articles also flag that the two-week timeline depends on prepared sites, reliable component supplies and energy infrastructure that can take years to build, so the claims remain untested at commercial scale.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line

stories.Headline: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Urban Renewal Authority will spend up to HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will check tender applications using automated AI systems. The move comes after accusations of corruption linked to the deadly Tai Po fire. The sum is a third of the HK$300 million the government allocated to the authority in its 2026-27 Budget. The funds are meant to reform the authority's Smart Tender scheme.

The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to give property owners an electronic platform for recruiting contractors. Its design anonymises the tender process, which is meant to prevent interference and encourage competition. However, the system cannot control who takes part in a tender exercise or who withdraws from one. The new subsidiary would bring in a professional team and build an automated workflow for deeper data verification and analysis. The authority said the approach would be "AI-first".

The authority's managing director is among those who have spoken on the plan, which is described as a direct response to the corruption concerns. According to the article, the director explained that the start-up money will go toward the new unit and its staff. The reporting quotes the director's account of the scope of the work, though the excerpt available is cut short. Further details on who else is accountable were not included in the material provided.

The plan sits within a broader government effort to restore public confidence after the Tai Po fire, which was deadly and which prompted questions about how renewal contracts were awarded. The articles provided do not say when the subsidiary will begin operating or how its performance will be measured. They also do not give a timeline for the wider reform of the Smart Tender scheme. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary - Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

stories.Headline: How Should Schools Adapt to AI?
stories.Summary:
Only one article was supplied, a transcript of a KQED Forum episode dated October 26, 2026, titled "How Should Schools Adapt to AI?" It describes a radio conversation rather than a breaking event, so the story below summarizes what educators said about AI in classrooms and is not a news report of a single incident. The discussion featured Daniel Herman, a humanities teacher at Maybeck High School in Berkeley, and Kip Glazer, principal of Mountain View High School and author of a guide for school leaders on AI. Herman said his classroom has changed little, but he has rethought assignments so they emphasize process over finished products, such as research presentations and interview projects that show students thinking on the page. Glazer described some teachers banning the technology while others admit they do not have all the answers, and she said students react to both approaches differently.

Herman argued that AI can be useful for learning but is poor at replacing a student's own thinking. Both educators stressed honesty and dialogue with students about whether and how they use chatbots. Herman said he asks students to tell him when they use AI, though he cannot confirm they all do. Glazer said some students avoid the tool entirely for fear of being labeled cheaters, and she pointed to students noticing when teachers use AI to grade work while forbidding it for students.

Glazer also raised concern about accelerating expectations, noting seventh graders contacting her about preparing for high school two years early. The episode included guests from Digital Promise, Alpha Schools and Prospect Sierra School, whose views were not summarized in the transcript provided. The host, Alexis Madrigal, framed the questions as open, asking how schools can gain AI's benefits without weakening students' reading, writing and critical thinking. The transcript ends before any firm conclusions are reached, so the articles do not say what schools will ultimately decide.

Articles.Title: How Should Schools Adapt to AI? - KQED

stories.Headline: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed California Senate Bill 903 on September 30, 2026. The bill would have prohibited companies from offering psychotherapy through artificial intelligence chatbots and would have limited how far clinicians could rely on AI tools. Supporters said the measure kept clinicians involved in patient care, while opponents said it would force clinicians to review and sign off on AI activity even when that activity was routine. Newsom said the bill was overly broad, invited a narrower version, and stressed the need for guardrails on AI in healthcare.

The veto leaves the national debate over AI's role in psychotherapy unsettled. Supporters argue that AI can expand clinician capacity and improve access to care, while lawmakers have cautioned against over-reliance and several states have acted to regulate it. Many states permit AI use in healthcare but have passed laws barring health plans from relying on AI for clinical decisions without clinician involvement. Some states also require providers or plans to disclose when AI is used in a patient's care or claims. The article's authors describe the resulting landscape as evolving, with new legislation expected in 2027.

State approaches to AI in psychotherapy vary considerably. Nevada bars AI providers from representing their tools as capable of psychotherapy and bars making AI mental health chatbots available, while Colorado forbids representing AI as a therapist and instead bars health plans from paying for AI psychotherapy services. Tennessee prohibits representing AI as a therapist without the further bans, and Illinois, Maine, Rhode Island, and Vermont require psychotherapy to come from a qualified professional. Utah expressly permits AI mental health chatbots if they disclose that they are AI. The rules on clinical use also differ, with Nevada generally limiting psychotherapists to administrative AI uses, while Colorado and Maine allow AI to make recommendations so long as a clinician reviews and approves the output.

Governor Newsom said that even with a review-and-approval exception, SB 903 went too far because it would limit clinicians' use of tools, including by requiring routine screening determinations to receive direct approval. Senator Padilla, the bill's author, said he would reintroduce the legislation in the coming session to prevent AI from providing psychotherapy. The 2027-28 California legislative session convenes on December 7, 2026, and the authors advise providers to monitor legislative developments in their jurisdictions. They also note that the requirements for AI-assisted psychotherapy could change substantially over the next year.

Articles.Title: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Drag queen explores legal action over AI-generated Jennifer Balkcom political ad
stories.Summary:
An Asheville drag queen known as Nova is exploring legal action over an AI-generated political attack ad that places her in a scene with Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager. The commercial was paid for by the National Republican Congressional Committee and approved by Republican NC-11 candidate Jennifer Balkcom, and the ad shows a barn dance in which Ager appears to dance with what looks like Nova. Nova told News 13 that she was blindsided when she learned her image had been used, and she says she has never met Ager or been to his property. She has sent a cease-and-desist order to Balkcom's campaign demanding the ad be removed. The ad continues to run on television and remains posted on YouTube.

Mike Tadych, a First Amendment attorney and counsel to the North Carolina Press Association, said that if the campaign ignores the cease-and-desist, Nova could have grounds for a misappropriation claim. He said the ad implies she was somewhere she was not, and that a cease-and-desist is only a first warning. If the ad keeps running after the campaign has been told there was no consent, Tadych said, Nova could file for damages and possibly seek an injunction. He also cautioned that political advertising receives strong First Amendment protection and that a court might be reluctant to order the ad taken down, since that could be treated as prior restraint.

Dr. Chris Cooper, chair of the political science department at Western Carolina University, said North Carolina has no law requiring political ads to disclose when artificial intelligence was used to create them, though many other states do. He said the ad may be meant to motivate Republican voters who oppose Ager to turn out. A spokesperson for Ager called the ad "100% fake" and said Balkcom "can't win on the truth." Balkcom's spokesperson had not responded to News 13's request for comment, and the story was published October 26, 2026.

Articles.Title: Drag queen explores legal action over AI-generated Jennifer Balkcom political ad - WLOS

stories.Headline: Human rights activists look to harness AI for the greater good
stories.Summary:
Human rights activists recently gathered at a hackathon to explore how artificial intelligence might be put to work for social good. The event brought together people who work on human rights causes and asked them to build technical tools while working through their doubts about the technology. Participants reportedly had to contend with a considerable amount of mistrust toward AI before they could begin building anything. The article describes the gathering as a place where that tension was openly discussed rather than brushed aside. The articles available to me do not spell out the specific tools the activists built, the number of participants, the dates of the hackathon, or any funding involved.

They also do not list particular outcomes, deployment plans, or measurable results from the event. What the coverage does establish is the central idea: activists were trying to find ways to use AI for the greater good despite reservations about it. Beyond that, the reporting is limited, so the details of what the hackathon produced remain unclear. The article does not name a specific person or organization held responsible for the event's conclusions, and it does not provide direct statements attributed to named participants in the material I have. The coverage is framed around the activists themselves and their effort to reconcile suspicion of AI with a belief that it might serve human rights.

Because no individual is quoted in the available text, I cannot report what any particular speaker said about their goals or their concerns. The broader context is a growing debate about whether technologies that raise concerns about trust, bias, and surveillance can also be turned toward protecting people's rights. stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: AI is knocking on banks’ doors — are defenses ready?
stories.Summary:
Recent cyberattacks on Korean financial institutions showed signs of artificial intelligence involvement, and some customer information was compromised. According to an analysis by a U.S. cybersecurity company, attackers connected an AI-powered security testing tool called Artex to multiple AI models. The article notes that the exact intrusion methods and the AI's role at each institution still need further investigation. Previously, hackers had to gather information, write programs and adjust their methods by hand after failures, but AI can now handle repetitive tasks such as identifying targets and testing weaknesses.

The author, a former president of KAIST, describes three technological shifts behind this change. The first is agentic AI, which receives an objective, uses tools and carries out multistep tasks rather than only answering questions. The second is the spread of open AI models and automation tools that can be downloaded and run independently. The third is that the same techniques serve both security researchers and attackers, so banks often can see only traces of activity, such as login records and program execution, rather than the instructions attackers gave their systems.

The author stresses that humans directed the attacks, so responsibility rests with those people, though developers and financial institutions should still be examined for their safeguards. The author proposes three responses. AI developers should treat safety as a basic product requirement, restrict permissions for risky actions and require human approval for potentially damaging steps. Banks should adopt Zero Trust defenses, which means segmenting internal systems, limiting access to what each person needs, and scrutinizing even legitimate accounts that pull unusually large amounts of data in short periods.

Governments should build systems for rapidly sharing information about attack methods and cooperate internationally to pursue cybercriminals who operate across borders. The article places these recommendations within a broader historical pattern, comparing AI rules to traffic lights and seat belts that followed earlier technologies. The author argues that AI cannot be governed by prohibition alone and that regulation should keep its benefits while limiting its risks. The article does not describe specific regulatory steps already scheduled, so what happens next remains unspecified beyond these calls for action.

Articles.Title: AI is knocking on banks’ doors — are defenses ready?

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania House passes bill requiring AI disclosure in healthcare
stories.Summary:
The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved House Bill 1925 on September 30, voting 144 to 59 to pass it. The bill sets rules for artificial intelligence in clinical care and in health insurance coverage decisions. Its disclosure rules cover healthcare facilities, and it limits how insurers may rely on AI during utilization review. The amended bill was referred to the Senate Institutional Sustainability and Innovation Committee on October 14 and remains pending in the Senate.

If enacted, the bill would require healthcare facilities, including imaging centers, to disclose their use of AI in clinical decision-making through website postings and written patient notifications. Those notifications would be needed once per episode of care rather than at every encounter. Facilities would also have to review AI system performance at least annually and make sure the technology does not override providers' independent clinical judgment. The bill extends disclosure requirements to certain personalized patient communications generated by AI.

It also covers Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program managed care plans, requiring that reviewers examine clinical records, document that review, and form their own judgment before issuing or upholding an adverse coverage determination such as a prior authorization denial. The articles do not name a specific sponsor or identify individual lawmakers who spoke for or against the bill. They report that the legislation is aimed at setting guardrails for AI in healthcare without hindering its development and adoption. The American College of Radiology has described state legislation as an important opportunity for radiologists and state medical societies to advocate for policies that protect patients and preserve physician decision-making.

The organization expects similar proposals addressing clinical AI during 2027 state legislative sessions. The proposed requirements could affect radiology practices that already use or plan to adopt AI in their workflows. The bill now moves to the Pennsylvania Senate, where it awaits action in committee. The articles do not say when the Senate might take it up or whether it will be enacted in its current form.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania House passes bill requiring AI disclosure in healthcare - Radiology Business

stories.Headline: AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege - New York State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association is offering a free webinar titled "AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege," scheduled for October 27, 2026, from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., and it is offered virtually as a webinar. The program covers two areas of concern for lawyers using artificial intelligence: fabricated cases and quotations, often called hallucinations, that have led to sanctions against lawyers and firms in California and New York, and the data-handling questions that arise before client-confidential information is entered into an AI tool. The sessions will be led by three panelists, Marc Lewis of San Francisco, Arlo Devlin-Brown of New York City, and Rhick Bose, head of U.S. operations at Crimson AI, with Nitesh Daryanani moderating.

The program is sponsored by the association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies, Committee on Technology and the Legal Profession, and Committee on Continuing Legal Education. It carries 1.0 credit in ethics and professionalism. The first session reviews recent sanctions decisions in both states involving AI-fabricated citations and examines the duties they implicate, including competence, candor toward the tribunal, and supervision. Panelists will compare New York's court rule on AI use with California's AI-focused amendments to its Rules of Professional Conduct, and they will discuss verification workflows for AI-assisted research.

The second session turns to confidentiality and privilege, looking at the obligations that apply when client information goes into an AI tool. It also considers how courts are beginning to address whether AI use affects privilege and work-product protection, and it covers what lawyers should look for in an AI vendor, including training on user data, retention, security, and contractual protections. The closing segment is an audience question-and-answer period followed by remarks from the moderator. The page lists a non-member price of $395.00, while association members may attend for free.

The association is the organizer of the program, and the articles name the panelists and moderator as the people presenting its content. The page itself does not describe any specific sanctioned lawyer or firm by name, and it does not report on any particular court ruling beyond saying that sanctions decisions exist. The page also advertises the association's Annual Conference 2027, with early-bird registration ending November 2. The article does not say what the outcome of any future court decision will be, and it does not indicate whether the regulatory approaches it compares are expected to change.

Articles.Title: AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege - New York State Bar Association

stories.Headline: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant
stories.Summary:
Bank of America has sent an email to customers, titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," warning them not to share their banking username and password with anyone else, including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on their behalf. The email was reported in a TechCrunch article published on October 27, 2026. A bank spokesperson confirmed the email was authentic after it was posted to social media. The warning comes as more customers hand their log-in details to personal AI assistants.

The article explains the risks of doing so. An AI assistant could take actions with someone's money without their knowledge. The bank might also treat the activity as an intrusion and lock the customer out of the account. A security flaw in an assistant could leak the credentials to others, including financially motivated hackers. The article also notes that account agreements at most banks make customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to, and the bank's email states that customers are responsible for activity resulting from that access.

The warning is directed at customers who use AI tools, and Bank of America is the institution that issued it. The article says banks are still working out how AI agents fit into finance and are reportedly dealing with unauthorized agents accessing customers' money. It also describes efforts by banks, payment providers and processors to decide how customers can connect AI tools to their accounts, including for agentic payments that let an agent buy things automatically at the best price or at a chosen time. The article does not say what steps Bank of America plans to take next or whether other banks will issue similar warnings.

Articles.Title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant

stories.Headline: AI Safety Emerges as Midterm Flashpoint in Battleground Races
stories.Summary:
Candidates in several of the country's tightest congressional races have begun making artificial intelligence a central part of their closing arguments, according to Bloomberg Law. Fears in Washington about AI disrupting the economy or threatening humanity are now spilling into the midterm campaigns, and a group of nominees has pledged to restrain the technology. The reporting, published on October 26, 2026, traces the shift to voters who are increasingly anxious about the subject. The coverage makes clear that the issue is no longer confined to policy circles.

Much of the spending so far has gone in a different direction. Congressional nominees have put nearly $17 million into AI-related television advertising this year, and most of that money has focused on concerns about data centers. A Bloomberg Government analysis of AdImpact data supports that figure. The article notes that a smaller set of candidates is taking a broader and more direct stance in some of the most closely watched contests. Those candidates are explicitly raising the risks and safety of artificial intelligence.

The articles identify the candidates themselves as the ones making these commitments, though the excerpts provided do not name them. In their campaign messages, they have said they intend to rein in the technology if elected. The reporting attributes these pledges to nominees in competitive districts rather than to any single party or institution. The excerpts do not include direct quotations from those candidates. What they convey is that the promises are part of how the candidates hope to persuade voters in the final weeks before the election.

The articles do not say how the races will turn out or whether AI will decide any of them. They also do not report any legislative or regulatory changes that would follow from the campaign pledges. Because the excerpts are cut off before the full text, further detail on individual candidates and specific proposals is not available here. The sources describe the trend as one that is still developing as the midterms approach.

stories.Headline: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips
stories.Summary:
Henkel, the German chemicals company, is producing semiconductor adhesives at its factory in Songdo, Incheon, South Korea, and the Korea Herald published a feature on the plant on October 26, 2026. The adhesives hold chips together, protect delicate connections and help dissipate heat, tasks that grow more demanding as AI requires more powerful processors and more complex packaging. The Songdo site, completed in 2022 after an investment of about 35 million euros ($39.2 million), is the only one of Henkel's four Korean factories that makes these materials. The facility covers 10,144 square meters and can produce up to 250 metric tons of semiconductor adhesive a year.

The plant operates under tight controls, with workers in cleanroom suits, temperature and humidity regulation, and ultraviolet light filtered out of some rooms to prevent unwanted chemical reactions. Its broader range covers more than 500 adhesive solutions for packaging, electronic components and device assembly. Production runs through seven stages, from raw material checks to mixing, testing and filling syringe-style containers, with about 100 barrel and cap combinations offered to customers. Henkel plans a new technical center in Seoul's Gasan Digital Complex, tentatively scheduled to open in March 2027, to expand its research work and coordinate with the Songdo plant. The company also says it is widening its portfolio for AI and high-performance computing, including its recently introduced Loctite Ablestik CDF900 series of thermally conductive die-attach films.

Hendrik Kohleick, Henkel's regional president for Asia-Pacific operations, described the Songdo plant as one of the company's major production sites for advanced packaging in the semiconductor industry and said it will strengthen cooperation with customers. Chang Ho-jun, president and head of Adhesive Technologies at Henkel Korea, said customers want adhesives that flow more easily and form thinner layers as chips shrink. Kim Young-mi, president of Henkel Korea, said the plant's role will grow in importance given the expansion of the global AI market and the strength of Korea's chip industry. The article notes that the site is near Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, that Incheon International Airport is about 30 minutes away, and that Henkel's Adhesive Technologies business generated about 10.7 billion euros in sales last year, compared with about 9.8 billion euros for Consumer Brands, which includes Persil.

Articles.Title: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips

stories.Headline: U.S. bill names N. Korea, Iran among countries of concern in AI cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
U.S. lawmakers have introduced a bill called the AI Cyber Defense Act, aimed at strengthening American cybersecurity against attacks that use artificial intelligence. The bill names North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba as countries of concern, according to congressional data reported on Monday, October 26, 2026. Representatives Pat Harrigan, a Republican from North Carolina, and George Whitesides, a Democrat from California, introduced it. It was referred to the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with private-sector AI stakeholders to develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing AI distillation attacks.

Within 180 days of enactment, NIST would have to establish a definition of these attacks and develop the related standards. AI distillation is a technique in which knowledge or capabilities from one AI model are transferred to another. The bill would also require NIST, within the same 180-day window, to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable focused on the defensive use of artificial intelligence for cybersecurity. The bill's sponsors are the two House members named above, and the measure has been sent to the House committee for consideration. The legislation itself is described as directing NIST's work, with the standards being voluntary rather than mandatory.

Congressional data was the source for the information on the bill's introduction and its named countries. The bill's introduction comes a week after the U.S. Treasury Department proposed expanding restrictions on American investments in sensitive technologies to include North Korea and several other countries. Washington is seeking to keep adversaries from using U.S. capital to develop advanced military capabilities. The report includes a graphic illustrating a North Korea-backed cyberattack threat. The articles do not say when the bill might move beyond committee or what the next steps would be.
