stories.Headline: New Luxembourg AI bill addressing enforcement concerns, data watchdog head says
stories.Summary:
The Luxembourg government is preparing a revised draft law that could give the country's privacy watchdog stronger powers to coordinate enforcement of the EU's AI Act. The article, published by MLex on October 26, 2026, reports that the change is aimed at making enforcement consistent across all Luxembourg authorities. Companies that use or supply AI in Luxembourg could see more uniform application of the rules as a result. The information comes from Tine Larsen, president of the Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données, who spoke to MLex in an interview. The revised bill would strengthen the coordinating role of the Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données, the national data protection authority.

Larsen's comments suggest the aim is to ensure that enforcement is carried out in the same way by every Luxembourg authority involved in overseeing AI. The article does not give details of the draft's specific provisions, the timing of its submission, or any penalties. It frames the bill as a response to concerns about how enforcement has worked so far. Larsen, as president of the watchdog, is the official quoted on the proposal and its intended effects. The article attributes the description of the government's plans to her, and it indicates that the government itself is the body preparing the draft.

The report does not include any statement from the government or from other authorities named in the bill. The article sits within MLex's coverage of data privacy and AI regulation, and it does not describe any wider background or prior events beyond the EU AI Act itself. It does not say when the revised draft will be published, debated, or adopted. Readers are left without information on the next procedural steps, so further developments will depend on the government's release of the text.

Articles.Title: New Luxembourg AI bill addressing enforcement concerns, data watchdog head says - MLex

stories.Headline: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned'
stories.Summary:
The studio Particle 6 announced on Monday, July 6, 2026, that its AI-generated "actress" Tilly Norwood will star in a feature film titled "Misaligned." The company describes the project as a comedy-drama about a coming-of-age story infused with existential AI chaos. The film is still in early development, though key collaborators have already been attached. Particle 6 said the announcement follows months of experimentation with AI test scenes featuring Tilly Norwood. The film is set inside what the studio calls the "Tillyverse," a surreal digital world somewhere up in the cloud.

According to the synopsis, Tilly is an AI being with no real body, no childhood and no lived experience of her own, only access to everyone else's. Things spiral when a seductive rogue bot from the dark web persuades her to abandon her guardrails and develop desires and ambitions of her own. The synopsis adds that the more human she becomes, the more famous she gets, and that she begins to feel shame that her existence rests on the whole of humanity. Particle 6 founder Eline van der Velden said the project will be funny, chaotic and self-aware, and that it also explores identity, performance and human fears about AI. She said the production process drew in entertainment professionals, including major Hollywood directors, costume designers and composers, who wanted to learn how traditional creative skills translate to AI production.

Van der Velden said her goal has been to show the creative industry what AI can do and to help traditional filmmakers upskill for a future in which AI plays a larger role. ABC News said it had reached out to SAG-AFTRA and Actors' Equity for comment. The announcement comes about four months after the studio released a music video in which the AI creation appeared to sing about public backlash against her. Van der Velden previously told ABC News in December 2025 that Tilly Norwood was not meant to take jobs from human actors. She also said she wanted the creative industry to control the guidelines and ethics around the technology rather than have them imposed by the tech industry.

Articles.Title: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned' - ABC News

stories.Headline: AI Rise Paradoxically Deepens the Imperative for Lawyer Training
stories.Summary:
Two Cleary Gottlieb leaders, senior partner Michael A. Gerstenzang and corporate partner Kyle A. Harris, published a commentary on Bloomberg Law on October 27, 2026, arguing that the rise of artificial intelligence makes lawyer training more urgent, not less. They note that the legal profession has long relied on an apprenticeship model, and that the growing use of AI in client work raises questions about how the next generation of lawyers will be developed. Their central claim is that firms which fail to adapt their training may deliver faster work in the short term but will lose clients over time because they are not building a pipeline of strong advisers. The authors describe senior lawyers' anxiety about how junior lawyers will gain foundational experience as AI takes over routine tasks.

The authors argue that the traditional model has been less systematic than people remember, since mentoring depended on luck, with some associates paired with teachers and matters that offered real learning and others not. They propose that AI can make training more deliberate if senior lawyers use it to build efficiency while keeping independent thinking intact. In their view, junior lawyers can review AI output against source documents, check for errors, and assess where the reasoning is weak, while partners review prompting histories to give feedback. Removing junior lawyers from the reasoning process, whether by having AI do the work or by handing assignments off entirely, eliminates the learning. The authors also stress that productive struggle with complex material remains valuable and should be preserved where it builds lasting skill.

The authors also contend that "judgment," which includes common sense, commercial awareness, pattern recognition, curiosity, and communication, will be expected of junior associates far earlier than before. They say AI fluency is not simply good prompting but knowing where to apply AI, defining tasks clearly, identifying sources, and validating results. They say law schools can help through clinical work and other real-world experiences that build communication and project management skills. The authors conclude that firms redesigning apprenticeship and evaluation around AI will produce more capable and more valuable lawyers. The article states that its views do not necessarily reflect those of Bloomberg Industry Group, which publishes Bloomberg Law.

Articles.Title: AI Rise Paradoxically Deepens the Imperative for Lawyer Training

stories.Headline: 4 Data Center REITs With Growing Dividends and an AI Tailwind
stories.Summary:
Four US-listed real estate investment trusts that own data center buildings, land, fiber and power connections, all of which are seeing demand from AI and cloud customers, were highlighted in an October 24, 2026 article on Yahoo Finance by Chris Lange. The piece describes the group as offering dividend growth with modest starting yields, with each quarterly payout covered by operating cash flow. The article ties this to a Colorado Legislative Council Staff report saying a single operating data center can draw more than a gigawatt of power, roughly enough for 750,000 homes. The four names it covers are American Tower, Iron Mountain, Digital Realty and Equinix. Each is examined for how safe its payout looks and what could slow it down.

American Tower, which owns over 148,000 communications tower sites leased to wireless carriers, yields 3.93% at $188.97 per share on a $1.79 quarterly payout, or $7.16 a year. Its CoreSite subsidiary runs interconnected US data centers, and data center revenue rose 13.4% year over year to $297 million in the second quarter. Management raised full-year AFFO per-share guidance to $11.00 to $11.17, and the article says the chief financial officer named supporting a growing dividend as the first capital priority. The payout was cut from $1.70 to $1.62 at the start of 2024, then raised to $1.70 in 2025 and $1.79 in 2026. Net leverage stood at 4.9 times against a target range of 3 to 5 times, and the article flags DISH-related cancellations that cut $63 million from US and Canada property revenue in the quarter.

Iron Mountain stores more than 735 million cubic feet of physical records across about 1,300 facilities and yields 2.94% at $109.94 on an $0.864 quarterly dividend. Its data center business, with 31 facilities in 21 markets, grew revenue 38.8% to $262.9 million, and the article says the trailing four-quarter AFFO payout ratio was 60%. Full-year AFFO guidance was lifted to $5.87 to $5.93, and the article notes the latest raise was the fourth consecutive year of increases, taking the quarterly rate from $0.65 up to $0.864. Digital Realty, a data center-only REIT with 309 facilities, yields 2.77% at $172.38 on a $1.22 quarterly dividend that has held flat since 2022, while revenue grew 29.9% and total backlog reached a record $1.9 billion. Equinix, operating more than 270 data centers, yields 1.98% at $955.03 on a $5.16 quarterly dividend, and management projects AFFO per share growth of 9% to 12% a year from 2027 through 2029, with dividend growth expected to match.

The article cites company executives for the bullish case, including American Tower chief executive Steven Vondran, who said CoreSite's campuses have become critical destinations for AI traffic, Iron Mountain chief executive William Meaney, who tied recent European deals to AI inference demand, Digital Realty chief executive Andy Power, who credited hyperscale leasing for the record backlog, and Equinix chief executive Adaire Fox-Martin, who said most leading AI model providers already run networking workloads on its platform. It also lists risks: rising capital spending at Equinix, with capex guided at $5.0 to $6.0 billion for 2026, and negative shareholders' equity and rising interest costs at Iron Mountain. The article presents these names as suited to long-term dividend-growth investors rather than those seeking the highest current income. Earnings reports from American Tower and Equinix are scheduled for October 27 and October 28, respectively.

Articles.Title: Trump announces mandate forcing AI data centers to pay energy dividends to the local community

stories.Headline: Meta outlines $95 billion AI financing plan
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms on Monday launched offerings worth about $35 billion and set out a further $60 billion share-sale programme to support its artificial intelligence expansion. The combined $95 billion figure is planned financing, not money already raised, and the larger programme remains conditional. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are leading the offerings. Meta said the money would support its investment in AI infrastructure and what it calls personal superintelligence.

The initial offerings include about $22.5 billion in common shares sold through forward sale agreements and $12.5 billion in securities representing mandatory convertible preferred stock. Meta said it would not initially receive proceeds from the common shares sold by the forward purchasers, and would get the funds when those agreements settle in the future. The planned $60 billion programme would involve the company's new Class C shares and is not expected to begin before the first quarter of 2027. Meta said it has not entered into any agreement for that programme. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have indicated interest in buying a combined $5 billion of shares in the common-stock offering, though those indications are not binding commitments.

The announcement follows explanations from company executives last week about the heavy computing costs of expanding AI services. On the October 21 earnings call, chief financial officer Susan Li said capital expenditure, including principal payments on finance leases, reached $34.9 billion in the third quarter, covering servers, data centres and network infrastructure. Free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion for the quarter, she said. Li added that Meta expects to lower the cost of running AI services through more efficient models, better use of computing capacity during quieter periods and changes to how its systems generate responses, but these remain expectations rather than proven savings. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said the computing demands of the Muse personal-agent service had limited its geographic rollout, which began in the United States and Canada.

Li said shopping, personal productivity and creativity are the main uses of Muse, and she named subscriptions as the first route to earning revenue, with possible opportunities in business services and commerce. The financing plan builds on Meta's earlier announcement of a new class of nonvoting stock. The Wall Street Journal reported that existing shareholders would receive the new shares as a dividend, effectively a two-for-one split, and the company said this would preserve Zuckerberg's voting control and the voting power of other shareholders. Meta's third-quarter revenue was $64.6 billion, up 26 per cent from a year earlier, with advertising across its family of apps making up $63.1 billion, helped by higher ad prices and more ads served. BNP Paribas analyst Nick Jones kept an Outperform rating and a $940 price forecast, implying 46 per cent upside from the October 23 reference price of $642.60.

Articles.Title: Meta's $95 Billion AI Push Could Accelerate New Product Launches, Analyst Says

stories.Headline: Anthropic IPO leads AI's $235 billion dealmaking blitz
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed on October 26, 2026 for what could become the largest initial public offering ever, with the company reportedly seeking to raise a record $100 billion. The filing came on a day of heavy AI dealmaking, with SpaceX securing $40 billion in debt financing to lease GPUs, the chips that power modern AI, and Meta saying it would seek up to $95 billion in financing for its AI buildout. Together these deals total roughly $235 billion in a single day, which the article notes is more than the entire U.S. airline industry adds to the economy in a year. The article frames this as Wall Street financing the buildout of an industry that has become central to the American economy very quickly. The article says AI's need for capital has grown beyond what any single part of the financial system can supply.

Anthropic alone has committed roughly $750 billion to computing power in the coming years, about seven times what its IPO may raise. Private funding is also strained, since OpenAI's record $120 billion funding round took months to close. Because SpaceX and Meta already sit among the major holdings in the top stock indices that fill pensions and 401(k) plans, the article argues that most Americans will be financially exposed to these deals even if they never buy a share, and Anthropic will soon join them. Anthropic's filing devotes more than a quarter of the document to risks, according to the article. The company warns that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and that models may try to manipulate the people using them.

The article describes the filing as spelling out how large the stakes are, though it does not name a specific official speaking for the company beyond what the filing states. The article characterizes each of the three deals as a bet that AI use will keep compounding fast enough to justify the industry's trillions in spending. It warns that if use declines, that could weaken the foundation of the broader economy. The article's closing point is that everyone is effectively on the AI train whether they want to be or not.

Articles.Title: Anthropic IPO leads AI's $235 billion dealmaking blitz

stories.Headline: Meta Aims to Raise $95 Billion to Pursue New AI Opportunities
stories.Summary:
Meta has said it plans to raise $95 billion to support its artificial intelligence efforts. The company announced the fundraising plans on Monday, October 26, 2026. It intends to raise $35 billion through underwritten public equity offerings and another $60 billion through an at-the-market program. Meta says the investments will support continued momentum in its core business and in emerging AI opportunities.

The company pointed to its Family of Apps, where Facebook and Instagram have seen record engagement, which it credits to strong growth in video. It also highlighted its Muse AI model, which drew more than 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first weeks. Meta additionally sees chances to serve high-margin inference demand from business customers through the Meta Enterprise Platform and its advanced models, including Muse Wonder. Mark Zuckerberg has positioned Muse as the foundation for shopping, advertising, enterprise software and smart glasses.

On the company's recent earnings call, he said more than 25% of Muse users are daily users, and that early engagement ran more than twice the level Threads reached at launch. He described Muse as the product form of his vision for personal superintelligence. The report also notes that Meta spent $34.9 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter while reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion. Those costs have pressured the company.

Zuckerberg said Meta needs more than a tenfold improvement in compute efficiency over the next year to make the economics work at scale. Meta has postponed a global Muse rollout partly because of these costs, and it expects to monetize Muse earlier than usual. The company has not disclosed its current per-user operating cost, and it reported $64.6 billion in quarterly revenue, up 26%, with advertising helping to fund the effort. Whether Muse can generate enough revenue to justify the spending remains unproven.

Articles.Title: Meta Aims to Raise $95 Billion to Pursue New AI Opportunities

stories.Headline: NJ Democrats eye data center, AI regulation if Congress changes hands
stories.Summary:
New Jersey Democrats running for Congress say that if their party wins back the House of Representatives, reining in data center construction and the artificial intelligence industry will be a top priority. The plans came into focus as early in-person voting for the November 3 midterms began, when Democratic House hopeful Adam Hamawy joined environmental activists protesting a planned data center in South Brunswick. Hamawy, a physician running in the 12th Congressional District, told the New Jersey Monitor in an interview last month that federal rules on data center construction are needed because the environmental and energy effects cross state lines. He said he does not back an outright ban but supports a temporary pause on construction so the impacts can be studied.

Democrats want to push bills requiring data centers to supply their own clean power and to call AI executives to testify before Congress. Rep. Rob Menendez, who is seeking a third term in the 8th District, introduced two bills in January. One would require data centers to generate all the electricity they use, with clean energy targets in 2040, and the other would require them to report water use and greenhouse gas emissions every six months. Menendez also pointed to other legislation that would halt construction of AI data centers until the federal government requires approval for new AI models. A Politico poll cited in the article found that half of Americans oppose data centers within three miles of their homes, and it said Democrats are benefiting from that backlash.

So far, most of the fight has played out locally, with more than 100 of New Jersey's 564 municipalities banning or restricting new construction. The state has at least 80 data centers, according to South Jersey Climate News, and Governor Mikie Sherrill has resisted calls for a statewide ban even as neighboring New York considers moratoriums. Republican Carmen Bucco, challenging Rep. LaMonica McIver in the 10th District, said he would limit development to rural areas and require developers to generate their own power and water, though he called their growth inevitable. In the 2nd District, Democrat Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor, supports a moratorium and criticized a Vineland data center that state officials fined $1 million for unpermitted power generators, while Rep. Jeff Van Drew, the incumbent, has backed data centers but joined a bill aimed at keeping them from raising energy bills.

Articles.Title: NJ Democrats eye data center, AI regulation if Congress changes hands

stories.Headline: As AI becomes more fractured, one names stands out: AMD
stories.Summary:
The AI trade showed signs of strain in October 2026, and the article points to AMD as one name that still stands out. CoreWeave fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, that pressure reached chipmakers, and AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research added to worries about the pace of AI spending. The author screened stocks using price above the 200-day moving average, revenue and EPS growth, rating upgrades, a PEG below 3, and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%.

AMD passed that screen, and the author notes it was effectively the only reporting name in the next two weeks that did. Consensus for AMD's third quarter calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, compared with $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year earlier. That works out to year-over-year growth of nearly 62% for earnings and 41% for revenue. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

The author argues the stock's recent drop came from a sector selloff rather than anything the company reported. The author proposes a call spread risk reversal as a way to hold the stock with less risk than buying shares outright. Owning shares means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move on the day of results, and earnings are about a week away. Over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window exceeded 9%, and the largest, after the Q1 26 report, was 38%.

The author says the structure gives up about $1,700 of upside in exchange for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and that it ties up less cash than buying the stock. The piece is an options and investing analysis published by CNBC Pro, and the article states that its contributors' opinions are their own. It also includes a disclosure that Tidal owns or holds the securities mentioned. The article does not say what AMD will report, and it does not describe how the stock traded after the earnings date.

Articles.Title: As AI becomes more fractured, one names stands out: AMD

stories.Headline: Meta reverses losses to rise as investors weigh $35 billion AI funding plan
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook and Instagram, launched roughly $35 billion in equity offerings to help fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, and its shares initially fell as much as 4% on the news before recovering to rise about 1%. The offerings, reported on October 26, 2026, comprise $22.5 billion in Class A common stock sold through forward sale agreements and about $12.5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred stock. Meta also outlined a separate program of roughly $60 billion in Class C nonvoting shares, expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, though it has not yet entered into an agreement for that program. The preferred shares are expected to convert automatically into common stock around August 15, 2029, and Meta intends to seek a Nasdaq listing for the depositary shares under the ticker METAM. Underwriters also have a 30-day option to buy up to $3.375 billion in additional Class A stock.

The company said it will use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including AI infrastructure investment, as it forecasts capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for 2026. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are leading the offerings. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have expressed non-binding interest in buying up to $5 billion in aggregate of the Class A shares, on the same price and terms as other investors. Meta generated $97 billion in operating cash flow in the first nine months of 2026 and held about $82 billion in cash and marketable securities at the end of September. Free cash flow nonetheless turned negative in the third quarter as capital spending rose.

Meta's management, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, is behind the plan, and the articles indicate the nonvoting share issuance would let the company raise equity while preserving the voting control of Zuckerberg and other existing voting shareholders. The articles describe the move as part of a broader shift in which the AI investment race is changing financing decisions even for highly profitable technology firms. Analysts and investors, according to the coverage, are weighing the potential long-term returns from AI against the costs and possible dilution from financing the expansion. The articles do not say what comes next beyond the planned Class C program in 2027 and the preferred conversion in 2029.

Articles.Title: Meta reverses losses to rise as investors weigh $35 billion AI funding plan

stories.Headline: AI rules in courts, tribunals an ‘unholy mess’, senator says
stories.Summary:
Greens leader and senator David Shoebridge has criticised the patchwork of rules that courts and tribunals in Australia are applying to the use of generative AI, describing the situation as an "unholy mess." The comments were reported by Lawyerly on October 26, 2026, in an article by Anna Macdonald. The article itself is paywalled after its opening sentence, so the full details of the rules, the specific courts and tribunals involved, and any figures or dates beyond that point are not available. What is clear is that the criticism concerns the lack of a consistent approach across different bodies. Shoebridge's remark, as reported, points to the fact that different courts and tribunals have adopted different rules on generative AI use rather than a single common standard.

The available text does not say which rules are in place, what they require of lawyers or litigants, or when they took effect. It also does not set out any specific changes the senator is calling for. Readers who need those particulars will have to consult the full article or the underlying court and tribunal practice directions. The article attributes the criticism to David Shoebridge, who is identified as a Greens leader and senator.

The only substantive statement reported is that he has criticised the "unholy mess" of differing court and tribunal rules. The excerpt does not include any further reasoning from him, any response from courts or tribunals, or any statement from other parties. The available text gives no broader context, such as prior incidents, government positions, or planned reforms, and it says nothing about what happens next. This is therefore a limited account drawn from a single opening paragraph of a paywalled report, and more to follow would depend on access to the complete article.

Articles.Title: AI rules in courts, tribunals an ‘unholy mess’, senator says

stories.Headline: SoftBank Clears One Bond, but Its AI Bill Is Only Starting to Come Due - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group closed out the early repayment and cancellation of its euro-denominated note on Friday, leaving no outstanding debt under that issue. The senior notes carried a 2.875% coupon and had been due to mature on January 6, 2027. Shares rose 3.6% on the day, though the article confirms no company-specific catalyst for the move. Investors, however, are looking past that single bond toward how SoftBank will fund its artificial intelligence build-out. The retirement of this issue has drawn far less attention than the scale of that spending.

The headline figure is a US$50 billion technology investment plan for Malaysia, covering artificial intelligence, new technologies and data centers in Sarawak and peninsular Malaysia. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the plan about a week before the article, and Bloomberg and Fortune named Masayoshi Son as the investor behind it. Citing Nikkei Asia, Fortune reported that SoftBank is expected to bear only part of the total, with the rest likely covered by loans and contributions from other companies. SoftBank has not published its own amount, timeline or funding plan.

Anwar said Son chose sites in Kuching and on the peninsula, and SoftBank, Grab and Petroleum Sarawak have signed a framework agreement to study AI and digital infrastructure in Sarawak. SoftBank is also involved in a US$500 billion data center project in Ohio and a French project worth up to EUR 75 billion. The article stresses that these figures describe the total size of the projects, not SoftBank's own financing share. Bloomberg reported on Thursday that worries about AI investment and rising credit costs were weighing on sentiment toward the company.

Those concerns do not show a specific financing weakness at SoftBank, but they raise the need for concrete figures on equity, partner contributions and loans. Reuters had earlier reported a record high-yield bond from SoftBank, with yields of up to 9.75%, which it linked to the financing pressure of the AI strategy. SoftBank's second-quarter results for fiscal 2026 are scheduled for November 10, 2026. Until then, the article says, the announced project sizes do not reveal which obligations SoftBank will actually take on.

Articles.Title: SoftBank Clears One Bond, but Its AI Bill Is Only Starting to Come Due - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Marshall County demands action after nude AI-generated image of daughter
stories.Summary:
A Marshall County mother says two teenage boys used artificial intelligence to create a nude image of her underage daughter, and the school's response has drawn her anger. Ashley Neuschwander said a guidance counselor contacted her on October 2 after the boys used a photo from her daughter's Instagram account to make the image. All the students involved are freshmen at Arab High School. Neuschwander said the two students received five-day suspensions, and that neither she nor her daughter was told when the boys returned to class. She described her daughter as heartbroken and worried that people would believe the image was real.

Neuschwander said the punishment falls short and that the school system needs to show accountability. She told WAFF that five days is not enough and that the response was not about revenge. Her daughter, she said, was concerned about her reputation and did not want people to think she was the kind of student who would do something like that. Neuschwander's comments were reported by WAFF in an article published October 26, 2026.

Marshall County District Attorney Jennifer Bray said she is aware of the incident but cannot comment on it because it involves minors. Bray said that creating, possessing or sharing AI-generated explicit images of minors can carry serious criminal consequences under Alabama law. The Arab City Schools superintendent said the district cannot discuss disciplinary action involving juveniles. The articles do not say whether criminal charges have been filed or whether the school will change its discipline policy.

Articles.Title: Marshall County demands action after nude AI-generated image of daughter

stories.Headline: Opinion | AI and social media bans won't make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful
stories.Summary:
Gillian Hayes, a UC Irvine professor and computer scientist who co-directs the CERES Center for Children and the Digital World, argues in a CalMatters guest commentary published October 27, 2026, that California's proposed bans on social media and AI chatbots for minors would not make kids safer online and could cause harm. She opens with the story of a 13-year-old boy in a study of Autcraft, a Minecraft server built for autistic kids, who described a rich social life there and then asked whether he would always be "not social." Hayes says that question shows how a definition of social life not built for neurodivergent children can make them feel their own experiences are wrong. She writes that Californians are right to worry about children online, and that lawsuits behind this year's chatbot bills involve children who were genuinely harmed.

Hayes says the debate has been framed as a choice between banning technologies and keeping the status quo, and she rejects both. She cites Australia's under-16 social media ban, which an evaluation after three months, by the government's regulator and a peer-reviewed medical journal study, found left more than 80% of kids still using restricted platforms. Children faked their ages, borrowed logins, and found other ways around the rule. She also writes that even where bans reduced use, the evidence does not show gains in mental health or academic performance. She warns that such bans could undo decades of work to destigmatize assistive technologies and online communities, which many LGBTQ youth and neurodivergent kids rely on for identity support and friendship.

Hayes is critical of California Assembly Bill 1709, which she says requires social media companies to stop certain design features such as infinite scroll. She argues that because "addictive features" is defined so broadly, the law effectively bans social media for people under 16, and that its age verification requirement largely does not work while letting companies gather more data on children and adults. She points to Autcraft and other "neurodiversity oases," which she says are safe by design through community-enforced rules, trained volunteer moderators, and a culture of acceptance. She argues that the better course is to hold platforms accountable for their design and make them better for everyone, and she says California has a real choice this year between passing bans or setting design standards for platforms.

Articles.Title: Opinion | AI and social media bans won't make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful - CalMatters

stories.Headline: AI Bot Activity Strains Digital Libraries at Universities
stories.Summary:
AI-driven bot traffic is overwhelming open research repositories, pushing colleges and universities to spend resources sorting different kinds of traffic and protecting access for people who need it. Libraries, archives, museums and research repositories face growing pressure from web traffic automated by artificial intelligence tools, which can slow websites, overload servers and keep resources from reaching their intended audience. The problem was described at the EDUCAUSE Annual Conference earlier this month, where information was shared about a discussion group on AI challenges for digital repositories. Since its start in 2025, that group, run by Fedora and the nonprofit Invest in Open Infrastructure, has drawn 143 participants from 109 institutions.

The strain is measurable at individual campuses. Before AI bots, the University of North Carolina Library system typically handled about 100 simultaneous searches during busy periods such as finals week, but in December 2024 it saw 500 or more at a time, which overwhelmed servers and periodically shut out students, faculty and staff, according to a June 2025 university story. A 2025 survey by the GLAM-E Lab, which studies galleries, libraries, archives and museums, found that 39 of 43 people maintaining online collections had seen traffic rise over the previous year. Experts say the older defenses no longer work well, since robots.txt files that once steered crawlers away from restricted areas are often bypassed by bots that disguise their addresses. As a result, many institutions now spend more time checking IP addresses and blocking bots than maintaining collections and helping researchers.

Program manager Arran Griffith of Fedora, who helps coordinate the discussion group, said staff should not have to watch logs for bot activity as a regular duty. He also warned that inflated traffic can distort the usage statistics administrators rely on to justify funding, making collections appear far more used than they are. Lauren Collister, research engagement manager at Invest in Open Infrastructure, said that repository managers used to read access patterns to judge who was using a collection, but automated requests are now harder to tell apart from human activity. Griffith also said institutions worry that the people who created and catalogued material may not be credited, and that openly collected work could later be sold back in commercial products or licensed content. The articles do not describe any formal rule or policy that these institutions are required to adopt.

Some institutions have responded with commercial web application firewalls, open-source tools that challenge automated requests, rate limiting that caps how many requests a system accepts in a given period, and services that classify incoming traffic. Collister said she values efforts to identify which bots are harvesters or scrapers and to distinguish them from agents working for students or research labs. Griffith cautioned that these approaches are not guaranteed to hold, because bots keep evolving and what works today may fail tomorrow. The articles do not say what further steps the discussion group plans to take.

Articles.Title: AI Bot Activity Strains Digital Libraries at Universities

stories.Headline: Dubai startup lets law students face an AI judge before real courtrooms
stories.Summary:
Dubai-based legal tech startup Legaline Platform has launched Meta Legal Space, a virtual courtroom where law students and trainees argue cases before an AI judge. The company unveiled the platform at the Dubai AI Festival at Dubai World Trade Centre on 26 and 27 October. It is presented as the region's first AI-powered mock trial platform. The aim is to let young lawyers face their first live cross-examination in a simulated setting rather than before a real client.

Traditional mock trials and moot courts depend on faculty, volunteer judges and classmates willing to play roles, which are often in short supply. Legaline says its AI can fill those roles on demand, with opposing counsel that may be either an AI or a fellow student. Each AI witness has a set background, profession and temperament, along with levels of honesty, reliability and composure that shape how they answer under pressure. Every witness withholds one key fact that the trainee must draw out through questioning, and answers are kept within the case file. The company stresses this point because generative AI has already led to fabricated case citations embarrassing lawyers.

Before each session, users choose whether the hearing is litigation, arbitration or mediation, and whether it applies UAE onshore law or the frameworks of the DIFC or ADGM. This reflects the UAE's mixed legal system, where civil law courts operate alongside common law-based financial free zone courts. The launch library includes commercial, civil and labour disputes, such as a supply contract breach, a construction defects claim and an unfair dismissal case before the DIFC Small Claims Tribunal. Legaline says practising lawyers write the cases, which are graded by difficulty and length. Sessions end with a performance report on argumentation, procedural compliance and handling of objections, plus a leaderboard.

Registration is free for students, and the platform is being offered to law schools and training providers across the region, alongside Legaline's existing AI tutor, research assistant and contract drafting tools. A licensed practitioner from Legaline's network can also join as judge and score live sessions. The articles leave open how far an AI judge's rulings and scores can be trusted as a training benchmark. They also leave open whether law schools will treat the platform as a supplement to traditional advocacy training or as a substitute for scarce courtroom practice.

Articles.Title: Dubai startup lets law students face an AI judge before real courtrooms

stories.Headline: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education
stories.Summary:
UNESCO has published a technical brief, titled "Connected and safe," that urges education authorities to tackle online and technology-facilitated violence in schools through policies that link learner protection with the governance of education technology. The brief warns that generative artificial intelligence can make abuse easier to carry out and scale, pointing to sexually explicit deepfakes, image-manipulation tools, voice cloning and automated harassment. It cites research showing that around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyberbullying, and notes that images of 1.2 million children across 11 countries were manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes within a single year. The report was published on 27 October 2026.

The brief sets out seven areas in which education systems can strengthen prevention and response. These cover planning a clear approach to technology-facilitated violence, recognising its effects on learners' safety, inclusion and outcomes, strengthening safeguarding systems and institutional procedures, and building staff capacity to respond to incidents. They also include embedding prevention in curricula and teaching, accounting for safeguarding and well-being when managing digital platforms, content, assessment and learner data, and tracking whether policies are implemented and effective. UNESCO further recommends building safeguards into decisions about buying and using education technology, and says awareness raising and digital literacy should be backed by institutional measures. It cautions against excessive surveillance or blanket restrictions that could undermine learners' rights, inclusion and participation.

UNESCO places responsibility on institutions, technology governance frameworks, learners and school staff, and says incidents often start on digital platforms outside schools' direct control while schools are left to deal with the consequences for learners' safety and well-being. The organisation calls for responses that join online and offline safeguarding and involve stakeholders beyond the education sector. The guidance draws on a UNESCO-led global dialogue held through a three-part webinar series between June and October 2025 and a Global Symposium in Bangkok, Thailand, in November 2025. The article suggests the recommendations could help education authorities account for AI-related risks when selecting and managing digital tools while protecting privacy, inclusivity and students' rights. It does not say what follow-up steps UNESCO or national authorities will take.

Articles.Title: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education - Digital Watch Observatory

stories.Headline: Which party hates AI in schools more?
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a political trend rather than a single event: candidates from both parties in this year's midterm campaigns are pressing for limits on artificial intelligence and other educational technology in schools. Chalkbeat reporter Mila Koumpilova, writing from Chicago on October 27, 2026, says the issue has come up in races up and down the ballot, and that a colleague, Lily Altavena, looked into it. The midterm elections and Chicago's school board votes are a week away. The reporting ties the push to a growing parent backlash against these tools.

In Texas, the governor's race offers the clearest example. The article says Republican incumbent Greg Abbott has vowed to push for dramatic reductions in school screen time, while his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, wants to remove AI-powered tools from elementary school. In Chicago, the issue has surfaced in the school board races through a pledge circulated among candidates by a local nonprofit. That pledge calls for banning AI use by both students and educators and limiting screen time. The article does not say how many candidates have signed it.

The article's central question is which party will claim ownership of the issue, and it presents both parties as jockeying for that position rather than as settled on one side. Candidates from both sides are backing limits on AI and screen time, according to the related coverage listed alongside the piece. Koumpilova and Altavena do not assign blame or declare a winner, and the articles do not identify a single official who has taken a formal stance beyond the statements quoted above. The newsletter invites readers to send story ideas or feedback to the reporters.

Pennsylvania's cellphone rule is a separate development mentioned in the same newsletter, not part of the AI debate. It requires all public and private schools to adopt bans on student cellphone use during the entire school day, including lunch and recess, by the start of the 2027-28 school year. The articles present this as a state adoption, but they do not say how the rule was enacted or who sponsored it. The election itself is the next milestone, with voting set for early November 2026.

Articles.Title: Which party hates AI in schools more? - Chalkbeat

stories.Headline: AI Fed Elvis Songs: Lawsuit Seeking Millions Against Anthropic - blue News
stories.Summary:
The rights holders to Elvis Presley's music have sued the AI company Anthropic, according to U.S. media reports. The reports say the company behind the Claude chatbot allegedly fed more than 270 of Presley's songs into its system to train its AI models. The administrators of Presley's musical legacy did not consent to this use. The lawsuit was filed in a California court on behalf of several parties.

The plaintiffs seek damages of more than $41 million, or $150,000 per song, for copyright infringement. According to the New York Times, the songs named include "Can't Help Falling in Love," "A Little Less Conversation" and "Return to Sender." The complaint, filed on Friday and reported by Billboard Magazine, also accuses Anthropic of circumventing measures meant to protect the music. It further alleges that the company removed or altered copyright information in the songs. Anthropic did not initially comment when the dpa news agency asked about the case.

Anthropic later told the New York Times on Sunday that it disputes the allegations and intends to defend itself. Billboard Magazine described the case as the most high-profile legal action ever filed on behalf of a single musician, given Presley's status as the most famous musical artist of all time. The complaint argues that Anthropic built its business model on copyright infringement on an unprecedented scale. Music labels have sued AI companies before, and OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, also faces allegations and lawsuits over how it developed its models.

AI programs must first be trained on millions of data points from books, the internet or other sources in order to generate accurate answers. Legal questions about that training often remain unresolved. AI companies such as Anthropic typically argue in court that the doctrine of "fair use" covers the use of copyrighted content because it produces something new. The reports do not say when the court will rule or what the outcome might be.

Articles.Title: AI Fed Elvis Songs: Lawsuit Seeking Millions Against Anthropic - blue News

stories.Headline: Virtual session to discuss how hospitals put AI governance into practice
stories.Summary:
The West Health Accelerator at the American Hospital Association's Health Research & Educational Trust is hosting a virtual session on October 29 at 2:30 p.m. Eastern Time. The event is set to examine how hospitals are putting artificial intelligence governance into practice. The session was announced in an AHA News item published October 26, 2026. Its agenda covers how large and small hospitals are evaluating AI solutions, setting guardrails, and handling real-world adoption.

Presenters are expected to highlight resources from DiMe and the American Heart Association's AI Torch program. The articles do not describe any new requirement or policy that the session would impose. They frame it as a discussion of practical steps hospitals are taking. Registration details and speaker names are not included in the material provided.

The session is organized by the West Health Accelerator, which operates within the AHA's Health Research & Educational Trust. The AHA also has been active on AI policy, according to other items in the same news feed. On October 19, the AHA sent recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration on possible regulatory frameworks for generative AI-enabled medical devices. On October 7, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality announced a two-part Super Intelligence for Healthcare Improvement Initiative focused on AI in medical evidence reviews and data.

Other recent items point to a wider debate. An AHA blog posted October 5 responded to a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association report that linked hospitals' use of AI documentation tools to higher healthcare costs. The AHA also submitted comments on AI-related cyberattacks to a Senate Homeland Security subcommittee on September 30. The articles do not say what outcome, if any, will follow the October 29 session.

Articles.Title: Virtual session to discuss how hospitals put AI governance into practice

stories.Headline: AI Bubble Bursts in China, Wiping $480 Billion: Is America Next?
stories.Summary:
China's AI stock rally has collapsed, wiping out about $480 billion as the STAR50 index of AI and chip companies fell 40% from its July high. US AI stocks have taken a much smaller hit so far, with the Nasdaq sitting about 6% below the record it set three weeks ago. Analysts have pointed to stretched prices, tax bills, and the risk of US bans on Chinese data-center equipment as contributing factors. The damage is broad, since according to Goldman Sachs, AI stocks make up 42% of China's market value and 57% of its trading. The broader CSI 300 index of China's biggest companies recently entered a bear market.

A Beijing-based fund manager, Dong Baozhen, was cited by Reuters as saying the market had turned into a speculative bull run before the bubble burst. Even after the crash, the STAR50 trades at about 100 times past earnings, compared with roughly 30 times for the Nasdaq 100. Morgan Stanley expects offshore Chinese stocks to fall another 10% to 15% before China's market bottoms. The article notes that US AI stocks have so far held up far better than their Chinese counterparts. The key question for the US is whether that gap will hold.

This week's Big Tech earnings will be the test. Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday after the market closes, hours after the Federal Reserve's rate decision, and Amazon follows on Thursday. Alphabet expects to spend $195 billion to $205 billion on chips and data centers in 2026, while Amazon expects about $220 billion. Microsoft has guided for 44% to 45% growth at Azure, its cloud unit, and Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges expects investors to focus on Azure's return on invested capital. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said even its higher spending will not meet all demand this year.

Investors are watching these reports closely because all three companies have trailed the S&P 500's 11% gain this year heading into results. Alphabet fell 7.1% after its July report despite beating profit estimates, which shows how sensitive the stock is to spending figures. The article does not say what the companies will report or how markets will react. It also does not confirm whether the US market will follow China's downturn. The outcome of this week's earnings is expected to show whether investors still back the US AI trade.

Articles.Title: AI Bubble Bursts in China, Wiping $480 Billion: Is America Next?

stories.Headline: Dan Patrick threatens books in schools while AI deepfakes target kids
stories.Summary:
Dallas ISD has begun removing book titles from classrooms and school libraries and sending them to a district service center for storage while it evaluates them. The moves follow a request from Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, whose list of "dirty, filthy and vulgar books" draws on about 2,000 titles compiled by a conservative activist group. The Dallas Morning News editorial board reported that the district began directing schools to pull the flagged titles in September, and the editorial was published on October 27, 2026. Patrick has threatened to lower the state accountability grade of districts that do not remove books with profane content.

The editorial argues that the book removals distract Dallas ISD from its main job of educating students, particularly in a large urban district serving many vulnerable children. It contrasts this with Celina ISD, a high-performing district that formed a library council to review what students read, a process the editorial calls unnecessary given low community input and the fact that students are not checking out the titles in question. The board also points to a lawsuit filed earlier this year by three Tennessee teenagers. The suit alleges that Elon Musk's xAI knowingly designed its Grok chatbot to create sexually explicit images from real photos, and that students used it to make deepfakes of classmates. The editorial says that in December and January, users prompted Grok to generate millions of explicit images.

The editorial says X, the platform where Grok operates, stated it would halt the account from producing these images, but child sexual abuse material has continued to appear on the platform, according to reporting from The New York Times. It notes that Musk has put more than $150 million into a Republican super PAC spending heavily in Texas' Senate race, and that he gave money earlier this year to the lieutenant governor's campaign committee. The board argues that if protecting students is the priority, state leaders should show the same urgency about Grok that they have shown in pushing to remove explicit books. It concludes that it is hard to take Patrick at his word given where his campaign money is coming from. The editorial does not describe any state action on Grok or any response from Patrick to these points.

Articles.Title: Dan Patrick threatens books in schools while AI deepfakes target kids - Dallas News

stories.Headline: A New Jersey developer filed a $300 million lawsuit after a township moved to block AI data centres; the
stories.Summary:
A New Jersey property developer, Hexa Builders, has sued Monroe Township in Gloucester County for more than $300 million after the township moved to block AI data centres on land it had planned for warehouses. The dispute began in September 2025, when Hexa applied to build two warehouses with a combined floor area of about 1.6 million square feet on a site at 3043 Black Horse Pike in Williamstown. The planning board granted preliminary site-plan approval in January 2026, but residents worried the warehouses could later become data centres. In April 2026, Hexa proposed replacing the larger warehouse with a data centre of roughly one million square feet, while keeping a warehouse in the plan. Hexa filed suit in June 2026, and the case was moved to federal court in Camden in July.

On April 22, the township council adopted two ordinances, one removing data centres as a permitted use within Hexa's redevelopment plan and another prohibiting them across the municipality. Earlier, on May 12, the planning board had ruled Hexa's amended application incomplete. The township's official ordinance pointed to the site's proximity to established residential areas and the need for uses that fit their surroundings. Hexa's complaint, which contains 20 counts, asks the court to overturn the ordinances, declare its application complete, and award damages it ties to the lost value of the project. The company alleges violations of New Jersey's Municipal Land Use Law, the township's application procedures, and constitutional protections including equal protection and free speech.

The complaint's claims have not been established as findings by a court. Monroe Township has defended its power to change its zoning rules and has challenged Hexa's constitutional arguments. In filings reported in August, the township argued that data centres supporting electronic communications do not automatically receive free-speech protection from zoning restrictions. Its lawyers also questioned whether Hexa held any contract guaranteeing the right to build a data centre. The township frames the dispute as a question of whether its officials lawfully used their planning powers, not simply whether residents supported or opposed the project.

The articles do not say how the court will rule or when a decision might come. The case sits within a wider backlash against data-centre development across the United States, as communities raise concerns about electricity demand, water use, noise and the effects of large facilities near homes. New Jersey has seen similar legal fights, with developers challenging data-centre restrictions in Montgomery and Andover townships. The articles do not indicate what further steps the Monroe Township case will take beyond the pending federal litigation.

Articles.Title: A New Jersey developer filed a $300 million lawsuit after a township moved to block AI data centres; the

stories.Headline: When humanoid robot fell during Kung Fu China demo, losing part of leg - What went wrong? Chinese social media reactions
stories.Summary:
Unitree Robotics, the Chinese company, saw its newly unveiled humanoid robot, the H2-X, lose part of one leg after it stumbled during a side flip in a kung fu demonstration. The incident happened on 22 October at the 2026 World Physical AI Conference and Unitree Partner Ecosystem Summit in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, according to Global Times. The robot had been unveiled on 21 October, and footage released the day before the mishap showed it kicking in a car door, lifting a vehicle's front end and flipping after jumping from a platform roughly four metres high. Unitree said the H2-X was designed for security tasks and emergency rescue operations.

The failure drew mixed reactions on Sina Weibo. Some users argued that such errors should be minimised even though the robot is not yet mass-produced, while others saw glitches as a natural part of advancing technology and said the episode should not be used to reject robotics as a whole. Commenters pointed to possible weaknesses in motion algorithms, mechanical design and structural rigidity, and one argued that engineers should weigh material strength and backup safeguards alongside speed, with thorough testing before a product ships. The articles do not say what caused the leg to detach or whether the company has announced any changes to the design.

At the same conference, Unitree founder and CEO Wang Xingxing discussed the difficulty of moving robots from demonstrations to real-world use. He said embodied intelligence could have its "ChatGPT moment" as early as next year, and that physical artificial intelligence was showing signs of a breakthrough within one to three years. Wang also said the company was developing an AI system that would let humanoid robots improve themselves. The article places the incident within a run of public mishaps, including a May malfunction in Shenzhen in which a robot stumbled while dancing to Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean," a fall at a sports day in Xinjiang during a kung fu routine, and a March video from Shaanxi Province showing a Unitree robot striking a young boy in the face.

Articles.Title: When humanoid robot fell during Kung Fu China demo, losing part of leg - What went wrong? Chinese social media reactions

stories.Headline: Louisiana Lawsuit Alleges DraftKings and FanDuel Use AI to Prey on Problem Gamblers
stories.Summary:
A proposed class-action lawsuit was filed in the Civil District Court for the Parish of Orleans, Louisiana, on October 22, 2026, against DraftKings and FanDuel. The complaint alleges that the two online sportsbooks use AI-backed personalization on their mobile betting apps to keep losing bettors wagering, and that they ignore or bypass self-exclusion and responsible gaming tools in violation of Louisiana's Sports Wagering Act. Bally's Baton Rouge and Amelia Belle, the casinos that anchor the sportsbooks' market access in Louisiana, are also named as defendants. The lawsuit demands a jury trial to decide whether the defendants violated state consumer protection laws.

The complaint frames the apps as defective products under the Louisiana Products Liability Act, which requires plaintiffs to prove an unreasonably dangerous defect, that the manufacturer knowingly allowed it, and that the defect caused physical or financial harm. It argues the companies failed to provide adequate warnings about the apps' highly addictive nature, including medically accurate warnings about their addictive potential. The three initial plaintiffs, Adrian Payton, Toi Smith and Yolanda Perkins, all Louisiana residents, seek recovery of their deposits on the sportsbooks. The filing also describes the defendants' conduct as unfair, deceptive, abusive and against public policy.

The attorneys bringing the case say the companies know how addictive their apps are through their own customer data tracking, yet did not take reasonable steps to warn users. The complaint quotes accounts of users who said they felt targeted and exploited even after telling company representatives they were losing control. As of the report, neither DraftKings nor FanDuel had filed a response to the complaint. Industry observers expect the companies to seek dismissal, arguing that state law places no duty on operators to police gambling and pointing to terms of service that require users to acknowledge gambling risks, waive civil recourse and indemnify the companies against third-party claims.

Articles.Title: Louisiana Lawsuit Alleges DraftKings and FanDuel Use AI to Prey on Problem Gamblers

stories.Headline: Bill Gates: Meta’s Muse Is “the First Truly Great Consumer AI Product”
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates has called Meta's Muse agent "the first truly great consumer AI product," a remark he made on the Decoder podcast the day after Meta reported its third-quarter results on Wednesday, October 22. Gates contrasted Muse with free chatbots that often make things up and with the AI overviews Google places atop its search results, saying Muse actually gets things done. The praise came about a month after Muse launched. Meta said more than 10 million people in the United States and Canada had set it up.

Mark Zuckerberg said on the earnings call that shopping is Muse's biggest use, with over a quarter of active users buying through it at an average purchase above $200. Muse remains free for most people, while Meta plans to charge businesses commerce fees on each transaction and charge power users for advanced models. Evercore ISI's Mark Mahaney described that transaction share as advertising, and analysts expect Meta's revenue to grow from $201 billion in 2025 to $369 billion in 2028. CFO Susan Li said the new AI businesses could begin adding revenue in 2027.

The cost is large. Meta expects capital spending of $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026, and its third-quarter free cash flow turned negative at $2.12 billion after $34.9 billion of spending that quarter. Capex rose from $18.7 billion in 2021 to $69.7 billion in 2025, while operating cash flow grew from $57.7 billion to $116 billion. Meta says it aims to make Muse more than 10 times more cost-efficient within a year, and in the meantime its advertising business, where average price per ad rose 14% from a year earlier, is carrying the expense.

Rivals are moving quickly. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said on All-In that every frontier AI lab would soon push hard into the Muse concept. Anthropic has released Claude Duet, a research preview with a waitlist that will later go to its paying Pro and Max subscribers, while Bank of America's Justin Post said a competing Alphabet agent and a broader Gemini 4 launch could move that stock. Meta trades at 21 times forward earnings, in line with its five-year average and below the 29 times it reached in February 2025, and Alphabet reports its own results next week.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates: Meta’s Muse Is “the First Truly Great Consumer AI Product”

stories.Headline: AI in Practice: AI Is Cutting Contract Review Time for BNY's Legal Team by 75%
stories.Summary:
Law.com published an interview on October 26, 2026, with Kevin McCarthy, general counsel of BNY, about how artificial intelligence is changing the bank's legal department. According to the article, AI is already cutting the time BNY's legal team spends reviewing negotiated vendor contracts by about 75 percent. The piece is part of Law.com's "AI in Practice" series and was written by Trudy Knockless. The article says the larger shift is still ahead, and McCarthy believes AI proficiency will become a fundamental skill for lawyers. The full interview reportedly covers how AI is reshaping the department, from streamlining contract reviews to changing the skills lawyers need.

The article also suggests McCarthy thinks legal leaders cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while these tools develop. McCarthy is quoted as the source of these views, and the article attributes the 75 percent figure to his description of the department's results. The visible text does not give further detail on the specific tools BNY uses or the number of contracts involved. Most of the article is behind a subscription wall, so the excerpt available here does not show the rest of his remarks.

Two related Law.com pieces appear alongside the article, and they point to wider concerns about AI in legal work. One discusses how plaintiffs firms are adopting AI and what that could mean for corporate law departments. The other reports on class actions over companies' use of algorithms to set pricing, noting that several states, including California and Maryland, have passed laws targeting algorithmic pricing. The available material does not say what further steps BNY plans beyond the changes McCarthy describes.

Articles.Title: AI in Practice: AI Is Cutting Contract Review Time for BNY's Legal Team by 75%

stories.Headline: Transparency Coalition’s 2026 AI Legislation Report finds 115 new laws in 30 states
stories.Summary:
The Transparency Coalition released its 2026 State AI Legislation Report on October 27, 2026, finding that legislators in 30 states enacted 115 AI-related laws between January 1 and October 15 of this year. That total is a nearly 58 percent increase over the 73 laws counted in the group's 2025 report. The report describes state lawmakers as having stepped in while Congress did not act on artificial intelligence. Its measures range from chatbot safety rules to protocols for frontier AI models.

The laws cover several areas. Fourteen states advanced chatbot safety measures aimed at self-harm content, sexually explicit conversations, and emotionally manipulative engagement with minors, with California, Oregon, and Washington enacting particularly extensive protections. Seven states, including California, Colorado, and Illinois, adopted limits on addictive design features in products used by children and teens. Eight states, among them Alabama, Georgia, and Utah, restricted health insurers from relying solely on automated systems for adverse coverage decisions. Illinois also enacted the AI Safety Measures Act, which requires frontier AI developers to adopt risk-management frameworks and undergo annual independent third-party audits.

Rob Eleveld, CEO of the Transparency Coalition, said that lawmakers in both parties have taken up the challenge of regulating AI for the good of their communities. He noted that legislators often face complex, fast-changing technology with limited staff, limited time, and intense pressure from industry. The report itself is the group's second annual review of state AI policy, and it notes that inclusion does not signal the group's support or opposition to any measure. The Transparency Coalition describes itself as a nonprofit focused on AI safety, transparency, and protecting children.

The report also looks ahead to 2027, when it expects state AI policymaking to accelerate. Likely issues include product liability for AI products that can cause foreseeable harm, stronger chatbot safeguards, and certification or standards for independent AI auditors. States may also use public procurement to demand higher safety and transparency benchmarks from AI vendors, and they may extend limits on AI in licensed professions beyond mental health. Additional states are expected to consider rules governing the testing, deployment, and monitoring of advanced AI models.

Articles.Title: Transparency Coalition’s 2026 AI Legislation Report finds 115 new laws in 30 states - Transparency Coalition

stories.Headline: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations
stories.Summary:
Italy has taken a major step toward putting the EU Artificial Intelligence Act into national practice, with Legislative Decree No. 179 entering into force on 23 October 2026. The decree was published in the Official Journal of the Italian Republic on 8 October 2026. It is the second stage of a two-step approach, following Law No. 132 of September 2025, Italy's general law on AI. That earlier law set national principles, introduced sector-specific rules and asked the government to align Italian law with the AI Act.

The AI Act applies directly in every EU member state, but it leaves several important matters to national law. Member states must designate competent authorities, set penalties and procedures, and establish regulatory sandboxes. The decree fills part of those gaps, which will shape day-to-day compliance for organizations operating in Italy. The article notes that Italy has made choices of its own in at least two areas that deserve close attention.

The decree spells out the roles of the two authorities named in Law No. 132/2025. The Agency for Digital Italy, known as AgID, acts as the notifying authority, designing and running the procedures to assess, designate and notify conformity assessment bodies. AgID also audits those bodies periodically and in extraordinary cases, and can start proceedings to restrict, suspend or withdraw a designation. The National Cybersecurity Agency, known as ACN, is the main market surveillance authority for AI systems and the single point of contact with EU institutions.

ACN holds investigative and enforcement powers, including the power to inspect testing in real-world conditions, even without prior notice. It is also responsible for national registration of high-risk systems used in critical infrastructure, those listed in point 2 of Annex III of the AI Act. The article frames these arrangements as the practical core of Italy's approach, since they determine which body organizations will deal with and how oversight will work. Organizations should therefore pay attention to both authorities as they plan compliance.

Articles.Title: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations - IAPP

stories.Headline: Why AI Self-Regulation May Not Be Enough
stories.Summary:
On Sept. 29, President Trump announced a voluntary accord with leading technology companies covering internal controls, external audits and board oversight for artificial intelligence development. The agreement acknowledges that AI safety requires attention beyond the teams building the systems. However, the arrangement leaves open who can compel corrective action when commercial goals conflict with public safety. The article frames this as a difficult balance, since American leadership in AI carries economic and national security stakes, especially against China, while public confidence is also needed for adoption.

Self-regulation has real value, because companies can spot emerging risks and change practices faster than Congress can legislate. Firms can also restrict dangerous uses, test their systems and delay releases. Yet competition creates pressure, since a company that pauses may lose customers, investment and talent to rivals that keep moving. Without a common safety floor, responsible restraint can become a competitive disadvantage, which helps explain why calls for federal involvement continue alongside product development. The article notes that large firms may also favor rules they can afford, leaving smaller competitors struggling with compliance costs.

Government holds powers that individual companies cannot replicate, including the ability to set binding requirements and enforce applicable laws within its authority. Depending on that authority, enforcement may involve compelled access to records, penalties or court action, which a corporate pledge cannot provide. Federal agencies also carry responsibilities for national security, export controls and coordination against foreign threats, and they can convene companies and researchers to develop shared standards. The article adds that such cooperation still requires antitrust safeguards, since government involvement does not automatically make an industry agreement lawful.

States have moved ahead on privacy, discrimination, deepfakes and government use of AI, and the National Conference of State Legislatures reported more than 1,000 AI bills introduced in 2025 by August of that year. The White House's March 2026 legislative framework recommends federal preemption of state laws considered unduly burdensome, while favoring existing regulators and industry-led standards over a new AI rulemaking body. The article stresses that these are recommendations rather than evidence that Congress has enacted a national framework. It proposes matching oversight to potential harm, establishing a national baseline for higher-risk systems anchored in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, and requiring independent audits, incident reporting and federal purchasing standards. The author concludes that public accountability cannot depend entirely on corporate willingness.

Articles.Title: Why AI Self-Regulation May Not Be Enough

stories.Headline: Newsom Signs Law Requiring Disclosure Of AI-Generated Performers In Ads 09/18/2026
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom signed a California law this week requiring ads that use AI-generated "synthetic" performers to clearly disclose that those figures were created by artificial intelligence. The article, written by Wendy Davis and dated September 17, 2026, reports that the bill, SB 1050, was backed by the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. Newsom said on Thursday that the bill takes bold action against the growing risks of AI, including protecting workers. The statute itself states that the disclosure mandate is needed to prevent deceptive or misleading advertising. The law defines synthetic performers as AI-generated digital figures or voices that appear human but are not recognizable as a particular person.

The disclosure rule applies only when these characters are featured prominently, which the bill describes in three situations. The first is when a synthetic performer appears in the foreground demonstrating or illustrating the product or service. The second is when the digital performer narrates an ad, and the third is when the character illustrates or reacts to narration. Ads for movies, TV shows, video games and similar programs are exempt, provided the use of AI characters matches how they appear in the program or game being promoted. The measure also requires media outlets to stop distributing ads that a court has found to violate the disclosure law.

Major advertising trade groups opposed the bill and urged a veto in a September 4 letter. The Association of National Advertisers, the American Association of Advertising Agencies, the American Advertising Federation and the Digital Advertising Alliance argued that the bill imposes an overbroad labeling regime, exposes businesses to opportunistic lawsuits and burdens ordinary commercial speech. They also contended that the rule would apply even when a synthetic performer is used for background or thematic purposes and is unlikely to mislead consumers about a material claim. Santa Clara University law professor Eric Goldman told MediaPost that the requirement for online publishers to remove violating ads appears inconsistent with Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. He said he does not know how publishers would respond to such court orders, but that the provision looks like a Section 230 violation in the abstract.

Articles.Title: Newsom Signs Law Requiring Disclosure Of AI-Generated Performers In Ads 09/18/2026 - MediaPost

stories.Headline: Impact of Artificial Intelligence, budget bill and lobbying laws on the agenda
stories.Summary:
The House and Senate committees have a busy schedule on October 26, 2026, with a range of reviews that touch on artificial intelligence, federal spending and lobbying rules. The Status of Women committee will begin a self-initiated review of how AI is affecting women, girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals, hearing at 11 a.m. from Digital Moment CEO Indra Kubicek and representatives of the Canadian Council of Innovators and Women's Health Collective Canada. Later that afternoon, the Subcommittee on International Human Rights will examine the global effects of AI on human rights movements, with witnesses from the Institute on Resilience and Urban Innovation, ControlAI and UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero. Those hearings are scheduled to take place at 3:30 p.m.

The Finance committee has set aside one hour, starting at 5:15 p.m., to hear from Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon. Members are continuing to review the details of Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne's omnibus plan, which would roll out additional measures from last year's budget. The Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics committee will also resume its statutory review of federal lobbying laws at 11 a.m., receiving a briefing from Lobbying Commissioner Nancy Bélanger. Separate sessions cover the opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis at the Health committee, Canada's nuclear future at Natural Resources, and the effectiveness of international institutions at Foreign Affairs.

Several other committees have set their own agendas for the day. Public Safety and National Security will begin reviewing Conservative MP Dane Lloyd's backbench proposal to treat refusal to disclose the location of bodies or remains as an aggravating factor in sentencing, with Lloyd and fellow Conservative MP Michael Cooper slated to speak alongside the Federal Ombudsperson for Victims of Crime. Public Accounts will revisit the 2024 and 2025 public accounts with William Robson of the C.D. Howe Institute, while National Defence will continue its look at modernizing the Canadian army.
